title: The State of Clean Energy Finance: 2026 Mid-Year Market Intelligence Report | Alfred Johnson
description:
I think we’ll look back at Q2 as the start of a new chapter of the supercycle in American clean and critical infrastructure.
The cycle kicked off in 2022 with substantially more policy support for clean power, manufacturing and associated supply chains.
New investors entered the market with different appetites for risk and those with higher return expectations looked to less served parts of the market, like clean fuels.
Crux ’s 2026 mid-year market intelligence report, released this morning, estimates that total clean energy and manufacturing capex reached approximately $74B in the first half of the year, on track for $180B by year’s end.
All of this against the backdrop of steadily rising energy demand and need for domestic supply chains.
text: I think we’ll look back at Q2 as the start of a new chapter of the supercycle in American clean and critical infrastructure. The cycle kicked off in 2022 with substantially more policy support for clean power, manufacturing and associated supply chains. The market hit a speed bump with the OBBBA in 2025. It took ~3 quarters for those changes to be absorbed and overwhelmed by an absolute deluge of capital for AI, rising electricity prices, technological innovation, and simmering geopolitical and trade tension. Q2 was a blockbuster. The highest ever for tax credit transfers. An uptick in manufacturing investment for the first time in six quarters. New investors entered the market with different appetites for risk and those with higher return expectations looked to less served parts of the market, like clean fuels. Preferred equity deals doubled in volume. Crux ’s 2026 mid-year market intelligence report, released this morning, estimates that total clean energy and manufacturing capex reached approximately $74B in the first half of the year, on track for $180B by year’s end. That’s more than the annual procurement budget of the DOD. The war in Iran disrupted oil supplies. We continue to compete with China for critical minerals and components, with political levers being deployed, as evidenced by the recently announced polysilicon tariffs. All of this against the backdrop of steadily rising energy demand and need for domestic supply chains. These macro factors are not going away, and they result in rising investment into real assets. A year ago, regulatory risk was binary: you invested or you sat on the sidelines. This year, investors priced risk and deal volumes stayed high: — 2026 tax credit pricing is lower where there is higher PFE risk (average 1.5 cents lower for ITCs, 2 cents lower for PTCs) — Change-in-tax-law provisions have moved from niche to standard since 2024, appearing in 55% of H1 2026 transfer agreements versus 12% in H1 2024 This market continues to grow year after year, because energy demand continues to grow year after year, and investors need to allocate to this much larger category. title: Anthro Energy breaks ground on $40 Million Louisville battery materials plant, creating 110 Jobs
description:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. — Anthro Energy has broken ground on a more than $40 million advanced battery materials manufacturing facility in Louisville, a project expected to create 110 full-time jobs and strengthen Kentucky’s growing role in the U.S. battery supply chain.
“K​​entucky continues to lead the nation in advanced manufacturing, and today’s groundbreaking marks another exciting step forward for our commonwealth,” Beshear said.
Anthro Energy expects to employ 110 people at the Louisville operation, including a range of skilled manufacturing and technical positions.
Anthro Energy previously established a production facility in California, where the company obtained battery certifications and began shipping commercial products.
For Louisville, the Anthro Energy project adds 110 permanent jobs and a $40 million-plus investment.
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. — Anthro Energy has broken ground on a more than $40 million advanced battery materials manufacturing facility in Louisville, a project expected to create 110 full-time jobs and strengthen Kentucky’s growing role in the U.S. battery supply chain.

Gov. Andy Beshear joined company executives and local officials Tuesday to mark the start of construction on what Anthro Energy says will be the first large-scale, U.S.-owned and -operated advanced electrolyte production facility in the country.

The Louisville operation will be Anthro Energy’s first commercial-scale manufacturing facility and is expected to produce more than 12,000 metric tons of advanced electrolyte material annually once fully operational.

The project, originally announced in January 2025, also is expected to support approximately 390 construction jobs as the facility is built.

“K​​entucky continues to lead the nation in advanced manufacturing, and today’s groundbreaking marks another exciting step forward for our commonwealth,” Beshear said. “Anthro Energy’s investment will create quality jobs for Kentucky families, strengthen our growing battery and energy storage sector and further establish Kentucky as the destination of choice for innovative companies building the future right here in America.”

Anthro Energy, founded in 2021, develops advanced materials designed to improve both the performance and safety of batteries.

The company’s proprietary injectable phase-change electrolyte, marketed as Anthro Proteus, can be used in batteries serving several industries, including automotive, defense, consumer products and micromobility.

Electrolytes are a critical component of batteries, carrying ions between the positive and negative electrodes. Expanding domestic production of battery components has become increasingly important as the United States seeks to reduce its dependence on overseas supply chains.

“As demand for advanced batteries continues to grow, rebuilding domestic manufacturing capacity for critical battery materials has become a national priority,” said David Mackanic, CEO and co-founder of Anthro Energy.

Mackanic said the Louisville project represents more than an expansion of the company.

“By producing advanced electrolytes here in the United States, we’re helping build a more resilient domestic supply chain while enabling the next generation of safer, higher-performing batteries,” he said.

Anthro Energy expects to employ 110 people at the Louisville operation, including a range of skilled manufacturing and technical positions. The jobs are expected to include production manufacturing technicians, process and control engineers, facility managers, accounting employees, maintenance workers and warehouse technicians.

The company also plans to develop partnerships with workforce and education organizations in Louisville and elsewhere in Kentucky to recruit and train employees. Potential workforce partners include KentuckianaWorks, Jefferson County Technical College, KY FAME, Fort Campbell and KY VALOR.

Louisville Mayor Craig Greenberg said the project adds another advanced manufacturing operation to the city’s industrial base. “This facility strengthens America’s battery and energy supply chain right here in our South End, and it’s a clear sign that Louisville is the epicenter for American advanced manufacturing,” Greenberg said.

Anthro Energy’s investment comes amid billions of dollars in battery, electric vehicle and advanced manufacturing investments announced across Kentucky in recent years. Among the largest are AESC’s $2 billion, 2,000-job battery gigafactory project in Warren County and Ford Motor Co.’s multibillion-dollar investments in Kentucky. Ford has committed $2 billion and 2,200 jobs to a Louisville project and another $2 billion and 2,100 jobs at the Kentucky 1 plant in Hardin County. Shelbyville Battery Manufacturing also announced a $712 million investment expected to create 1,572 jobs in Shelby County, while Toyota has announced a $1.3 billion investment in Scott County.

The projects are helping establish a broader battery and advanced-mobility supply chain across the state, one that extends beyond battery-cell manufacturing into materials, components and related technologies. Anthro Energy’s Louisville plant adds an important piece to that supply chain because its focus is on the electrolyte technology used inside batteries rather than vehicle assembly or battery-cell manufacturing.

The Louisville investment also reflects the city’s efforts to attract advanced manufacturing operations tied to automotive, defense and emerging technologies. Trevor Pawl, CEO of One Louisville, said Anthro Energy’s move from project announcement to groundbreaking in less than a year demonstrates the region’s ability to move advanced manufacturing projects forward. “This is a project that strengthens our national energy supply chain and creates real opportunity for Louisville workers building the batteries that power our defense, mobility and automotive industries,” Pawl said.

The company also has a Kentucky connection. Anthro Energy’s co-founder and chief technology officer is a Kentucky native and University of Kentucky graduate. Anthro Energy previously established a production facility in California, where the company obtained battery certifications and began shipping commercial products. The Louisville investment will take the company into commercial-scale production.

For Louisville, the Anthro Energy project adds 110 permanent jobs and a $40 million-plus investment. For Kentucky, however, its broader significance may be the addition of another link in the domestic battery supply chain as the state works to translate its recent wave of battery and electric-vehicle investment into a larger advanced-manufacturing ecosystem.

description:
EPA 2027 engines: Owner-operators worry over recent regs proposals Daimler Truck North America-owned engine manufacturer Detroit recently confirmed it will fully transition its North American heavy-duty diesel lineup to EPA 2027-compliant engines at the start of 2027.
[Related: 'Not gonna be a guinea pig': Owner-ops wary of maintenance unknowns with EPA 2027] Equipment owners responding to Overdrive polling feared the worst from additional complexity: greater maintenance costs.
Read more about Detroit’s EPA 2027 engine rollout plans in Cannon’s report here.
NHTSA’s recall number for the Volvo recall is 26V-513.
NHTSA’s Mack recall number is 26V-515.
text:
EPA 2027 engines: Owner-operators worry over recent regs proposals

Daimler Truck North America-owned engine manufacturer Detroit recently confirmed it will fully transition its North American heavy-duty diesel lineup to EPA 2027-compliant engines at the start of 2027.

As reported by Overdrive sister publication CCJ’s Jason Cannon, proposed updates by the Environmental Protection Agency to its 2027 emissions regulations would allow engine manufacturers to pay non-conformance penalties as a short-term alternative if they cannot immediately meet the hardware standards, and grant manufacturers more time to validate the reliability of new emissions-control systems under real-world operating conditions.

A number of OEMs have announced plans to take advantage of the reprieve, among them Paccar and Cummins, Cannon noted, the latter of which will introduce its new HELM platform engines -- the X10 and X15 -- through a gradual production ramp-up starting in January 2027. Select current-generation engines will stay available during the transition.

Among other changes that remain at proposal stage from EPA are an end to DEF-fault-related engine derates, likewise rollback of extended warranty requirements for emissions systems in the 2027 diesel regs. In response to recent polling, Overdrive's owner-operator readers showed little favor for the warranty-period-rollback part of the proposal.

What favor they did show was expressed in the form of the 42% who felt EPA didn't go far enough and should cut the 2027 diesel regulation entirely.

"A good warranty says a company believes in the product," noted one polling respondent, elaborating the view expressed by 42% of owners that EPA should keep the warranty extensions. "A longer warranty says the company really means it."

Speaking during Daimler’s Q2 2026 earnings presentation, Chief Executive Officer Karin Rådström and Chief Financial Officer Eva Scherer confirmed that the manufacturer will phase out its current 2026 engine platform in favor of a newly engineered powertrain built to meet the more strict standard.

Detroit is utilizing a pre-selective catalytic reduction (pre-SCR) system. Positioned upstream of the primary aftertreatment system (ATS), this helps the engine reach operating temperatures faster. Since the pre-SCR system introduces DEF ahead of primary aftertreatment, it takes advantage of exhaust heat before the ATS gets to operating temperature. Hardware and functionality are nearly identical to the SCR in use since 2010.

Rather than relying on higher-cost electrical additions or paying regulatory fines for higher-emission engines, Daimler’s technical solution, Rådström said, achieves compliance while minimizing structural complexity.

[Related: 'Not gonna be a guinea pig': Owner-ops wary of maintenance unknowns with EPA 2027]

Equipment owners responding to Overdrive polling feared the worst from additional complexity: greater maintenance costs.

"A huge part of the cost of operating a modern truck is repairing the federally mandated emissions," noted one respondent. The owner urged EPA to better balance "reasonable repair time" with a "reasonable life cycle" required of the emissions system.

EPA's recent proposals would also roll back useful-life requirements for manufacturers in the 2027 regs to the 2030 model year.

Read more about Detroit’s EPA 2027 engine rollout plans in Cannon’s report here.

[Related: Volvo, Mack end 5-mph DEF derates | Cummins' MY 2027 engines getting phased rollout]

Roof marker light issue prompts Volvo, Mack recalls

Volvo Trucks and Mack Trucks are recalling more than 2,300 trucks combined for an issue that could cause the roof marker lights to not illuminate.

According to National Highway Traffic Safety Administration documents, the recalled trucks may be equipped with roof marker lights that may not have appropriate connector housing lengths. This can result in the center marker lamp connection failing and the light not illuminating.

As a result, the trucks fail to comply with the requirements of Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard number 108, "Lamps, Reflective Devices, and Associated Equipment."

Volvo’s recall includes 1,851 model year 2027 Volvo VNL and VNR units. Mack’s recall includes approximately 513 model year 2027 Mack Pioneer and Anthem trucks.

Dealers will replace the center roof marker light, free of charge. Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed Oct. 5. Owners can contact Volvo Trucks' customer service at 800-528-6586 with recall number RVXX2608. NHTSA’s recall number for the Volvo recall is 26V-513. Owners can contact Mack's customer service at 1-800-866-1177 with recall number SC0498. NHTSA’s Mack recall number is 26V-515.

International recalls trucks for windshield wiper issue

International Motors has issued a recall for approximately 49 trucks due to an issue that could result in inoperable windshield wipers.

The recall includes certain 2027 HV, HX, LT, MV, and RH trucks in which a retaining nut in the wiper assembly may loosen, causing both windshield wipers to disconnect from the motor.

title: LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI See ESS Revenue Share Near 30% as EV Demand Slows
description:
At Samsung SDI, the ESS revenue share is expected to increase from 20.6% in the second quarter to 35.1% in the fourth quarter.
The main drivers of the shift in revenue mix are the expansion of AI data centers and increased investment in power grids in North America.
Both companies are converting EV battery production lines to ESS production in response to changing market conditions.
Samsung SDI posted an operating profit of 203.8 billion won in the second quarter, returning to profitability for the first time in seven quarters.
However, Chinese manufacturers still hold a significant share of the North American ESS market, while automakers are also moving into the ESS business.
text:
AI Data Center Power Demand Drives ESS Growth as Battery Makers Shift Production From EVs

The share of energy storage systems, or ESS, in the total revenue of LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI is expected to rise from the 20% range in the second quarter to the mid-30% range by the end of the year. Demand for ESS is growing as power consumption from artificial intelligence data centers surges in North America, while battery makers are accelerating the conversion of production lines to ESS products to offset slowing electric vehicle demand.

According to battery industry sources and securities analysts on Aug. 17, ESS accounted for 28% of LG Energy Solution’s revenue in the second quarter, up steadily from 22.7% in the fourth quarter of last year. ESS revenue is projected to rise to 2.98 trillion won, or approximately $2.11 billion, in the third quarter and 3.85 trillion won in the fourth quarter, pushing its share of total revenue to an estimated 37.3% in the fourth quarter. At Samsung SDI, the ESS revenue share is expected to increase from 20.6% in the second quarter to 35.1% in the fourth quarter.

The main drivers of the shift in revenue mix are the expansion of AI data centers and increased investment in power grids in North America. ESS demand, which was previously driven largely by conventional power-generation projects, is increasingly shifting toward large-scale and long-duration systems as AI data centers expand. LG Energy Solution secured more than 3 trillion won in new ESS orders during the first half of this year, including projects involving AI data centers.

One example is the Steel River Energy Project in Arkansas, being developed by Google and U.S. power-generation company CCE. LG Energy Solution is supplying batteries for the 2.9-gigawatt ESS project, which will be combined with 2.5 gigawatts of solar power generation. Industry analysts expect higher plant utilization to translate directly into improved earnings as the cost burden from production-line conversions in the first half subsides.

Both companies are converting EV battery production lines to ESS production in response to changing market conditions. Samsung SDI began operating part of an EV battery production line at its Indiana joint venture with Stellantis after converting it to produce nickel-cobalt-aluminum-based ESS batteries in the fourth quarter of last year. More recently, Samsung SDI acquired Stellantis’ stake in their joint venture with General Motors and plans to build its first wholly owned battery plant in North America, including production lines for ESS batteries.

LG Energy Solution plans to establish five major ESS manufacturing hubs in North America and aims to secure more than 50 gigawatt-hours of local production capacity by the end of this year. In addition to its plants in Holland, Michigan, and Ontario, Canada, the company has recently begun producing ESS cells at its joint venture plant with Honda in Michigan and at its Ultium Cells plant in Tennessee. It plans to begin producing pouch-type lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, batteries for ESS this year and expand into prismatic LFP batteries next year.

Patent litigation targeting Chinese battery makers and U.S. policy support are also expected to provide a boost. LG Energy Solution recently filed patent infringement complaints with the U.S. International Trade Commission against Chinese battery maker EVE Energy and others. The move is seen as part of the company’s effort to strengthen its position in the global battery market beyond power tools and EVs. Rising patent risks for Chinese-made batteries could encourage global automakers to source more batteries from South Korean suppliers.

On the profitability front, tax credits under the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act are expected to play a key role. Samsung SDI posted an operating profit of 203.8 billion won in the second quarter, returning to profitability for the first time in seven quarters. In addition to a one-off benefit from tariff refunds, the results reflected benefits from the Advanced Manufacturing Production Credit, or AMPC, supported by increased North American production. Analysts expect AMPC benefits to expand as local production increases, potentially supporting a structural improvement in profitability.

However, Chinese manufacturers still hold a significant share of the North American ESS market, while automakers are also moving into the ESS business. An industry official said companies that secure large-scale production capacity ahead of an upturn could gain an early lead in the market, adding that earnings visibility could improve further as supplies of LFP batteries ramp up in the second half of the year.

title: 'Gift to the fossil fuel industry': RWE relinquishes North Coast offshore wind lease, part of ...
description:
RWE is one of two companies, alongside Vineyard Offshore, that hold wind leases off California’s North Coast through its RWE U.S. Offshore subsidiary.

Elsewhere, other offshore wind companies have already caved to the pressure.
This is yet another example of how off the rails the Trump Administration has gone.
text:
‘We the people are paying for this buyout, and what we get in return is more expensive energy, backwards climate policy and greater harm to our communities,’ said Assemblymember Chris Rogers

On Thursday, renewable energy company RWE announced that it entered into a $1.22 billion agreement with the Trump administration to relinquish its offshore wind leases. RWE is one of two companies, alongside Vineyard Offshore, that hold wind leases off California’s North Coast through its RWE U.S. Offshore subsidiary.

According to a press release published by RWE Thursday morning, the company’s settlement with the U.S. Department of Interior will “resolve claims against the U.S. government and relinquish its offshore wind leases off the coasts of New York, California and Louisiana.”

“RWE U.S. Offshore secured these leases from the U.S. government with a long-term commitment to develop offshore wind capacity in American waters and invested more than $1 billion toward the leases and the development of these projects,” RWE’s release reads. “These leases provided legal rights to develop offshore projects and represented years of planning, investment, and partnership with federal agencies.

“After careful consideration, it was determined there is no path forward to permit these projects in the U.S. for the foreseeable future. The settlement resolves RWE U.S. Offshore’s legal claims and provides $1.22 billion in settlement funds. The company determined that this resolution best serves the interests of its stakeholders and allows it to direct resources toward energy projects that can be advanced with certainty.”

The news did not come as a shock.

“Today’s news is disappointing but not surprising,” Environmental Protection Information Center Executive Director Tom Wheeler told the Times-Standard via an emailed statement Thursday morning. “The Trump Administration has used its full weight to hamper offshore wind development. Elsewhere, other offshore wind companies have already caved to the pressure. The winners today are the fossil fuel industry and the losers are Humboldt County and the planet. But tomorrow is a new day. The Trump Administration will end. And the promise of offshore wind remains: clean, reliable energy built locally by well-paying blue-collar jobs. The Trump Administration can delay, but it cannot suppress the future.”

RWE’s press release says that the agreement will allow the company to “redeploy its capital to accelerate value-accretive opportunities that deliver reliable and affordable energy.” That “redeployment” is described as including “$900 million to acquire an indirect 16% stake in the Louisiana LNG Project” — a large-scale natural gas development that has been criticized as a major source of greenhouse gas pollution — and other natural gas projects throughout the U.S.

“While RWE’s shareholders get their bag, the rest of us get the finger. We the people are paying for this buyout, and what we get in return is more expensive energy, backwards climate policy and greater harm to our communities,” Assemblymember Chris Rogers told the Times-Standard via email Thursday morning. “The Trump Administration is again using taxpayer dollars to settle personal vendettas and line the pockets of his friends and donors by protecting oil profiteers from the competition of clean, affordable and renewable energy.

‘Every American should be enraged.’

U.S. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-San Rafael), ranking Democratic member of the U.S. House of Representatives’ Committee on Natural Resources, released a statement Thursday morning just before noon, calling the DOI and RWE’s agreement a “fake settlement” and saying that “the deals are deeply corrupt and illegal” and “when the accountability comes, and I promise you accountability is coming, everyone involved in them will answer for it.”

“The most corrupt, lawless administration in American history is once again flouting the law and attempting to use over $1 billion in taxpayer dollars to kill off clean energy projects slated to create thousands of good jobs and lower electricity bills for Californians,” Huffman said. “Trump is strongarming companies into taking these illegal deals and abandoning offshore wind projects that would put huge amounts of cheap electricity on the grid and lower electricity prices. Instead, he is pressuring them to invest not only in dirty fossil fuel projects, but in LNG export facilities that push domestic energy prices even higher at a time when American families are reeling from skyrocketing costs caused by his reckless war of choice in Iran.

“One of the projects illegally canceled in this fake settlement is off the coast of Humboldt County in my district. The benefits of that project were tremendous — revitalizing the economy of a rural community, creating thousands of quality jobs and lowering utility bills for families all across California. Like a mob boss, Trump tightened the screws on RWE and, shamefully, the company capitulated and went along with this sham deal that robs the American people and makes a mockery of RWE’s stated commitments to clean energy. When these illegal, fake settlements are reversed by the courts and/or future congressional action — and they will be — RWE and others who participate in these charades will own every bit of the shame they deserve.”

Huffman said that the total cost to the taxpayers for paying companies to abandon offshore leases already ads up to “the tune of about $4 billion” noting that such settlements have thus far employed funding intended for the payout of federal lawsuits and settlements.

“Trump is using the Judgment Fund as a slush fund to pay for it. This is the same pot of taxpayer money Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche tried to use for his so-called ‘Anti-Weaponization Fund’ to pay off convicted J6 felons,” Huffman said. “Once again, we see this administration’s priorities laid bare: treating a fund that exists to resolve valid claims and liabilities as a massive personal slush fund Trump can use to reward criminals, kill off clean energy projects and do virtually anything else that serves his personal and political interests.”

Spokesperson Anthony Martinez from Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office provided the Times-Standard with the following statement: “The pattern is impossible to ignore. After getting beaten in court again and again, Trump has stopped trying to win on the merits and continues to make backroom deals to kill clean energy projects — a gift to his fossil fuel industry donors at the expense of America’s economic security.

“While China and other global competitors race to dominate the technologies that will power the future, California is building a modern grid, energy independence and an energy future that Trump is too small to understand.”

“This action by the Trump Administration is utter BS,” Sen. Mike McGuire (D-Healdsburg) said in an emailed statement delivered around 1 p.m. “The overall California RWE wind project would have advanced clean, reliable wind energy — enough to power 5 million homes — and created good rural jobs for the North Coast. Seemingly ripped from a script of VEEP, Trump is now forcing RWE’s hand to reinvest in the same fossil fuels which delivered the climate crisis to our door. This is yet another example of how off the rails the Trump Administration has gone. Total buffoonery.”

The Interior Department provided a statement from Secretary of the Interior and Chairman of the National Energy Dominance Council Doug Burgum Thursday afternoon.

“Americans deserve an energy system built on common sense, not one dependent on costly subsidies or technologies that can’t meet our country’s current demand,” said Burgum. “We welcome RWE’s agreement and voluntary investment in projects that strengthen our nation’s energy security, provide dependable baseload power, and help keep electricity affordable for hardworking Americans today while supporting our country’s long-term energy future.”

By: Robert Schaulis

text:
Mining giant BHP says it intends to trial “dynamic charging” technology for the two electric haul trucks that it is testing at its Jimblebar mine in the Pilbara, and is also taking delivery of another two battery electric locomotives for testing in the current financial year.

BHP has been criticised for its slow progress on the switch to electric mining equipment at its giant iron ore mines in the Pilbara, in contrast with the ambitious plans of rival Fortescue that intends to reach “real zero” and eliminate all diesel use at its mines by the end of the decade.

BHP has stated on a number of occasions that it does not consider the technology is ready for widespread deployment, although it has been trialling two Caterpillar 793 XE Early Learner battery-electric haul trucks at its Jimblebar mine.

In a statement to the stock exchange this week along with its annual results, BHP said that it expects to commission high-power static charging infrastructure and Caterpillar’s Dynamic Energy Transfer technology at the Jimblebar test facility this year.

The company actually announced plans to use the DER technology back in 2024. The technology uses a rail to charge electric haul truck’s batteries while the machine is on the move, and the system’s infrastructure is flexible, which allows it to be easily relocated.

BHP says it started working with Caterpillar to deploy zero-exhaust emissions mining trucks in 2021, but its slow progress in Australia is blamed by analysts and competitors on the huge rebates that it – and the rest of the mining industry – receives each year from the federal government from diesel use.

Climate Integrity reported on Tuesday that BHP pocketed around $548 million in fossil fuel subsidies under the Fuel Tax Credit (FTC) Scheme in the 2026 financial year, when it reported an after-tax profit of US$9.83 billion (A$13.8 billion).

Climate Integrity says that despite acknowledging that “diesel displacement is the largest lever” it has to reduce operational greenhouse gas emissions, BHP’s diesel use has increased year-on-year. It estimates that the amount of diesel BHP used across its operations increased from 1.23 billion litres in 2024/25 to 1.25 billion in 2025/26 – enough to fill 500 olympic swimming pools.

It will receive an estimated $548 million in Fuel Tax Credits from the federal government for the last financial year – less than the estimated $622 million BHP claimed in 2024/25 because of the halving of the fuel excise after the diesel price surge in response to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

BHP would have received an estimated $648 million in fuel tax credits in 2025/26 without the halving of the excise,” Climate Integrity said.

“Half a billion dollars in fuel tax credits flowing to a company posting a $13.8 billion profit is a policy failure,” Climate Integrity Executive Director Claire Snyder said in a statement. The Fuel Tax Credit scheme was never designed to subsidise the world’s largest mining companies while they delay decarbonising their fleets. It’s time for reform.“

“BHP itself says diesel displacement is the single biggest lever it has to cut emissions – and yet its diesel use keeps climbing. It’s hard to see why it would move any faster while taxpayers are quietly picking up half a billion dollars of their fuel bill every year.”

Fortescue has also argued for fuel tax credit for big miners be capped at $50 million a year, saying that the estimated $3.4 billion paid out each year is not giving any incentive to switch to electric trucks and other mining equipment quickly.

Fortescue is well on the way to delivering a green grid to power its iron ore mines, and the electric equipment it is installing, including more than 300 giant electric haul trucks, electric excavators, bulldozers, water carts and loaders.

BHP, meanwhile, also announced it has commenced trials of two Wabtec battery-electric locomotives in Port Hedland and took delivery of two Progress Rail battery-electric locomotives for testing in FY27.

“Once locomotives from both OEM’s are in trial, we expect to be one of the first mining companies globally to conduct side-by-side evaluations of battery-electric heavy-haul locomotive technologies from two suppliers within the same operating environment,” the company said.

Initial market analysis suggests $0.38/W MIP for modules would therefore raise the bottom of the imported-module market by approximately $0.14/W.
The Secretary and CBP can also restrict imports by a company and its affiliates if the Secretary determines that a company is stockpiling polysilicon or polysilicon derivatives before Dec. 4, 2026.
Section 232 Is Likely to Remain a Significant Energy-Sector Risk Alongside Other Tariffs This polysilicon action will likely not be the administration’s last use of Section 232.
text:
The Trump administration has added another significant layer to U.S. solar trade policy and supply chains, further complicating the costs of procurement. The White House issued a presidential proclamation Aug. 6 under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, establishing minimum import prices (MIPs) for polysilicon and several downstream products, additional tariffs on polysilicon derivatives and an incentive program intended to spur investment in U.S. manufacturing.

The administration determined that imports of polysilicon and derivative products threaten to impair U.S. national security, pointing to polysilicon’s role in both semiconductor and solar products production, as well as national defense programs and artificial intelligence (AI), and the decline in U.S. production capacity. According to the proclamation, the U.S. share of global polysilicon production capacity declined from approximately 50% in 2005 to less than 2% in 2024 and that the U.S. share of global semiconductor wafer fabrication capacity decreased from 37% in 1990 to 10% in 2024.

The new remedies take effect Dec. 4, 2026, for goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, giving developers, manufacturers, importers and financiers approximately 120 days to evaluate their exposure.

What the New Section 232 Regime Does

At the center of the proclamation is a new set of minimum import prices:

The proclamation relies on two annexes detailed below to provide specifics on the covered products and implementation of the MIP and ad valorem tariff.

Annex I identifies the specific Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) classifications covered by these price floors. They include high-purity polysilicon; several categories of polycrystalline and monocrystalline silicon wafers; photovoltaic cells; photosensitive semiconductor devices, including photovoltaic cells; and photovoltaic modules. The annex cautions that its product descriptions are informational and that the HTSUS classifications determine the legal scope.

Annex II implements the measures through new Chapter 99 HTSUS headings and makes an important point: certain covered products are subject to both the Section 232 MIP and the applicable ad valorem tariff, in addition to existing applicable HTSUS duties. All anti-dumping and countervailing duties and other applicable charges also continue to apply.

For most covered ingots, wafers, cells and modules, the 15% ad valorem tariff is imposed in addition to the MIP and applicable Column 1 duties, which provides duty rates for most countries. Column 1 countries either have a trade agreement with the United States or otherwise qualify for normal trade relations (NTR) status. Nearly all countries are eligible for these duty rates.

Raw polysilicon alone, though, is only subject to its MIP but not the ad valorem tariff. Certain trading partners also receive different treatments. Products from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Switzerland and Liechtenstein are subject to a structure under which the applicable Column 1 duty and the additional Section 232 tariff rate together sum to 15%, while covered United Kingdom products face a sum totaling to an additional 10% instead of 15%.

To ensure thorough enforcement of the new rates, the proclamation closes the common foreign trade zone (FTZ) rule that allows goods to be admitted into the zone without immediately being formally entered into U.S. customs territory. The proclamation eliminates that benefit, except for certain merchandise eligible for domestic status within an FTZ, by requiring that products admitted to an FTZ on or after the proclamation's effective date must be admitted under "privileged foreign status" and products already in an FTZ under that status be subject to the new MIP-ad valorem regime when that merchandise is eventually entered into the U.S. for consumption.

To avoid application of these new rates in full, importers can take steps to certify that they qualify for an MIP exemption or adjusted MIP, or for drawback claims.

The specified MIP rates will not apply if an importer provides documentation certifying that any “first arm’s-length sale” of the covered products in the United States will occur at or above the applicable MIP and one of three conditions is met:

Used in U.S. manufacturing rather than resold: If the imported product will not itself be resold, the downstream product made from it will be sold at or above the MIP applicable to that product.

Resold in the United States: If the imported product will be resold, its U.S. resale price must be at or above its applicable MIP.

Preexisting fixed-term contracts: An imported product can also qualify where it will be resold pursuant to fixed terms under a time-limited contract entered into before Aug. 6, 2026, provided the MIP threshold concerning its entered value is also satisfied.

If the sale price provided is below the applicable MIP, then an importer will be charged a supplemental rate equal to the difference between the value of the product provided and the applicable MIP (e.g., $0.22/W for a cell minus a sale value of $0.15/W is equal to a supplemental rate of $0.07/W).

Certain products can otherwise qualify for a manufacturing drawback claim under subsections (a) and (b) of Section 313 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which enables a company to obtain a refund of certain duties paid when that merchandise is used in U.S. manufacturing and the resulting goods are subsequently exported or destroyed. For these new Section 232 duties, drawback is available only if:

The product is not of a type covered by an AD/CVD order. Importantly, the proclamation looks to the type of merchandise covered by an antidumping or countervailing duties (AD/CVD) order, not merely the country from which the particular shipment originates. If that type of merchandise is subject to an antidumping or countervailing duty order, the proclamation says it is ineligible regardless of whether the particular article came from a country named in the order.

The article comes from a specific Trade Agreement Partner. The proclamation specifically designates the United Kingdom, European Union, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Mexico and Canada, plus countries that subsequently conclude qualifying trade and security agreements with the United States.

All polysilicon contained in the article must itself originate in a Trade Agreement Partner country. This adds a supply-chain tracing requirement beyond simply determining the origin of the finished cell, module or other derivative product.

The MIP May Matter More Than the Headline 15% Tariff

For solar developers, the principal near-term concern may be the price floor itself.

Initial market analysis suggests $0.38/W MIP for modules would therefore raise the bottom of the imported-module market by approximately $0.14/W. Similar estimates suggest that the cell MIP could increase low-end cell pricing by roughly $0.11/W and that the $100/kg wafer MIP translates to approximately $0.15/W, roughly $0.10/W above recent imported-wafer pricing.

While the 15% ad valorem tariff does not necessarily mean that a $0.38/W module must now be sold to a customer for approximately $0.44/W, the broader effect will nevertheless likely be an upward repricing of the U.S. module market. Exactly how much manufacturers ultimately pass through will depend on contracting and market conditions. Manufacturers offering products with greater U.S. content or lower exposure to Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC), antidumping and countervailing duty risks have been able to command premiums over the cheapest imports, but raising the price floor for those imports could give other suppliers additional room to increase pricing as well.

Additional Incentive to Onshore

The proclamation also authorizes an onshoring incentive program for companies that commit to building, refurbishing or expanding U.S. production of polysilicon and derivative products and begin construction by Jan. 20, 2029. Approved companies may receive relief from certain Section 232 duties on imports associated with those investments. Notably, module manufacturing capacity is not included among the eligible manufacturing categories, focusing the incentive farther upstream in the supply chain.

What Developers and Financiers Should Watch

The first issue is existing procurement contracts. Developers should review module and component supply agreements closely for tariff-change provisions, change-in-law clauses, customs valuation requirements and responsibility for newly imposed duties. Annex II recognizes time-limited, fixed-term contracts entered into before Aug. 6, 2026, within its documentation framework, but it does not provide a blanket exemption from the new regime.

That makes allocation of tariff risk particularly important for projects with fixed-price power purchase agreements (PPAs). One initial market estimate suggests that a $0.10/W increase in module prices could require approximately $4/MWh to $5/MWh in higher PPA pricing to offset the added module expense. Projects that have locked in revenue but not equipment costs could consequently experience pressure on financing assumptions, debt-service coverage and returns.

Lenders and tax credit investors are also likely to place greater emphasis on procurement certainty. Financing models should consider not only the initial MIPs but also the proclamation’s authorization for the Secretary of Commerce to adjust those price floors if market conditions change.

The proclamation also directs the Secretary of Commerce and U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agency to monitor for fraudulent documentation and stockpiling activities. CBP is authorized to permanently prohibit an importer and its affiliates from importing covered polysilicon and products into the United States if their documentation was materially inaccurate or the importer materially failed to comply with its certification. CBP may also impose penalties on the noncompliant importer. The Secretary and CBP can also restrict imports by a company and its affiliates if the Secretary determines that a company is stockpiling polysilicon or polysilicon derivatives before Dec. 4, 2026.

Developers should assess the polysilicon Section 232 risks alongside FEOC requirements, domestic-content qualification, AD/CVD and other tariff risks and now the FCC foreign-produced inverter restriction rather than analyzing each regime separately. An imported module could now be more expensive and also carry FEOC or AD/CVD duty risks, while a higher-priced domestic product may offer additional value through domestic-content qualification and reduced trade-policy exposure. Procurement decisions will increasingly depend on a project’s entire tax, trade and financing profile rather than headline module price alone.

Importer compliance will also matter. The proclamation contains substantial documentation and enforcement requirements tied to U.S. resale pricing. For financed projects, diligence regarding supplier compliance, customs representations and contractual remedies may therefore become increasingly important.

Section 232 Is Likely to Remain a Significant Energy-Sector Risk Alongside Other Tariffs

This polysilicon action will likely not be the administration’s last use of Section 232. The administration has increasingly relied on the statute to protect domestic manufacturers within supply chains it views as economically or strategically important. Several tariff determinations relevant for the renewable energy industry have been issued so far while a couple remain in process or have been left open while the U.S. Department of Commerce and the administration assess market conditions, trade negotiations and domestic production responses.

As discussed in a recent Novogradac analysis of tariffs facing renewable energy and storage, this means developers need to consider not only tariffs already in force but also potential follow-on Section 232 action. Investigations also do not always produce an immediate across-the-board tariff. Some have instead resulted in narrower initial measures and the reservation of authority to impose additional restrictions if domestic capacity or trade conditions do not develop as expected, or open-ended monitoring. That flexibility makes Section 232 particularly difficult to model over a multiyear project-development timeline.

At the same time, tariffs intended to bolster domestic manufacturing can create meaningful costs for other domestic industries. Solar, wind and battery projects often consume large volumes of imported equipment, components and materials, meaning measures designed to strengthen one U.S. industry can increase capital costs for another. The administration has shown some willingness to modify tariff regimes when downstream impacts become sufficiently significant, but its broad shift away from renewables and attempts to halt projects and divest suggest that exemptions, product exclusions, negotiated arrangements and adjustments to rates could be out of reach.

Nor should renewable energy developers assume these trade restrictions would disappear under a future Democratic Congress or administration. Protection for strategic domestic industries has increasingly enjoyed bipartisan support due to rising concerns among lawmakers and industry particularly on Chinese competition, global supply chain dominance and infiltration of the U.S. energy system.

It is more likely, rather, that a Democratic administration amends existing tariffs. The Biden administration, for example, retained significant elements of the first Trump administration’s Section 232 steel and aluminum framework while modifying its application to allies, and it substantially increased Section 301 tariffs on Chinese solar cells, polysilicon, wafers, batteries, critical minerals and other strategic products.

A future Democratic administration or Congress could therefore potentially amend Section 232 and related tariff regimes where policymakers conclude that the measures are excessively punitive to downstream U.S. industries, including solar, wind and battery developers, rather than to eliminate those protections wholesale.

For developers and financiers, tariffs, particularly Section 232 tariffs, should therefore increasingly be treated as a durable project-development cost and risk and rather than a temporary feature of the current administration. Industry experts are already speculating that the new restriction on foreign-produced inverters issued by an executive interagency working group and the Federal Communications Commission’s order could likely lead to an additional Section 232 investigation into imported inverters.

Join policy and industry leaders at the Novogradac 2026 Fall Renewable Energy Tax Credits Conference, Nov. 5-6 in Washington, D.C., for timely insights on clean energy policy following the Nov. 3 congressional midterm elections and opportunities to connect with key industry partners.

title: If Trump wants to lower costs, he should override this California port rule
authors: Sam Raus, opinion contributor, Sam Raus, opinion contributor
description:
California’s “green” port regulations are affecting a large chunk of imported goods that ordinary Americans buy on a daily basis.
If the Trump administration wants to lower costs for consumers, repealing this Environmental Protection Agency waiver should be an immediate priority.
California admits that the rule costs billions, with the state estimating that compliance costs will exceed $2.2 billion through 2032.
The American people cannot afford to pay the bill of California’s environmental extremists.
If the administration is serious about making life more affordable, California’s port mandate should be on the chopping block.
text:
Families across America are still feeling the squeeze of high prices, from groceries and gasoline to mortgage payments and childcare. And nonsensical environmental policies enacted by the Biden administration are keeping those prices high, hitting the supply chain of these critical markets before essential goods reach customers.

California’s “green” port regulations are affecting a large chunk of imported goods that ordinary Americans buy on a daily basis. One of the Biden administration’s most expensive climate regulations remains in effect, giving California permission to impose billions of dollars in new shipping costs. Since California’s ports move nearly 40% of America’s imports, these costs don’t stay in California — they show up in higher prices nationwide.

If the Trump administration wants to lower costs for consumers, repealing this Environmental Protection Agency waiver should be an immediate priority.

The California Air Resources Board’s Vessels At-Berth regulation forces ships to plug into shore power and use costly approved equipment, aimed at reducing carbon emissions, or else face a steep fine. While implemented at the state level, this policy exists only as a result of the Biden EPA granting a waiver allowing it.

These are expensive compliance costs that jack up the prices on consumer goods for Americans without reducing toxic waste or other harms to the local environment. California admits that the rule costs billions, with the state estimating that compliance costs will exceed $2.2 billion through 2032.

But every extra dollar imposed at the port eventually shows up on store-shelf price tags. As transportation of goods becomes more expensive, those costs are passed on to the consumer through higher prices — whether it be clothing, appliances, construction materials or toys.

Fortunately, the Trump administration has the power to overturn this through the Congressional Review Act. EPA can revisit the waivers given to California and overturn the implementation of the Vessels At-Berth rule.

As this administration hones in on the issue of affordability, with its moves to undo burdensome regulations on energy markets, housing development, healthcare and more, this waiver reversal is an obvious policy to act on. The American people cannot afford to pay the bill of California’s environmental extremists.

Washington cannot promise to fight inflation while leaving unnecessary regulatory costs in place. Repealing this waiver won’t solve every inflation problem, but it is one practical step toward eliminating billions in avoidable supply-chain costs. If the administration is serious about making life more affordable, California’s port mandate should be on the chopping block.

text:
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) has formally filed to intervene in the proposed merger of Dominion Energy with Florida-based NextEra Energy.

The $67 billion merger proposal is under review by Virginia’s State Corporation Commission (SCC). According to her office, Spanberger is the first governor in Virginia history to intervene in an SCC case. Chief Energy Officer Josephus Allmond, the first person appointed to Spanberger’s new cabinet position, also filed to be a party in the case.

In the filing, Spanberger cited her administration’s core policy of providing “an affordable, reliable, local, and clean energy system.”

“As Governor, I remain skeptical of the benefits this merger would deliver to Virginia — particularly if those benefits come at the expense of affordability, existing jobs, or meeting our homegrown clean energy goals,” Spanberger said in a statement. “By formally intervening in the SCC case, my Administration will be able to directly advocate on behalf of Virginians impacted by what would be the largest utility merger in U.S. history.”

As parties to the case, Spanberger and Allmond will be able to share concerns and request more information about the proposed merger. The governor’s filing outlined three “non-negotiable priorities” she is seeking: providing more affordable energy bills, protecting the utility workforce and accelerating plans for affordable and reliable clean energy.

Dominion Energy is Virginia’s largest electricity utility company, serving about 2.7 million customers in the commonwealth, as well as nearly 1 million in North Carolina and South Carolina. Next Era is North America’s largest electric and energy infrastructure company, serving 6 million customers in Florida.

Dominion Energy says union employees would receive 18 months of job protection after closing, while non-union employees would receive two years of current pay and comparable benefits. The merged company would maintain dual corporate headquarters in Richmond and Juno Beach, Florida, as well as an operational headquarters in Cayce, South Carolina.

“It preserves the Dominion Energy utilities our customers know — the same local leaders, employees, regulatory oversight and commitment to an all-of-the-above energy mix — while adding capabilities that can help us build needed infrastructure more efficiently and keep bills affordable,” Robert Blue, chair, president and CEO of Dominion Energy, said in a release. “Our employees and communities can be confident that we will remain a strong local employer, a constructive economic development partner and a reliable provider of the energy that powers homes, businesses and new investments.”

Prior to intervening in the Dominion Energy-Next Era case, Spanberger also pressed the SCC to shift more of the cost of new electric transmission capacity onto large load users. The SCC then ordered Dominion Energy to develop a tariff to assign more costs for new infrastructure onto data centers.

Spanberger’s second in command, Lt. Governor Ghazala Hasmi, is holding a listening tour around Virginia about the proposed merger and energy costs. Multiple state lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have pushed Spanberger to hold a special session so the General Assembly can adopt policies allowing the SCC hearing process to extend past six months.

The merger case will last about six months after the joint petition for acquisition was filed with the SCC. Nov. 2 will be the last day to file as a public witness before testimony will be given on Nov. 5, 9 and 10. Written comments are also being accepted. The evidentiary hearing involving parties in the case is expected on Nov. 17.

There is an 180-day review period from the merger’s July 15 filing date, which would mean an SCC decision could come by Jan. 11, 2027.

Along with Virginia’s SCC, the merger is being considered by the North Carolina Utilities Commission, the Public Service Commission of South Carolina, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

If state and federal regulators approve the merger, the companies expect closing would happen in the second half of 2027.

text:
WASHINGTON, DC— Minnesota Governor Tim Walz signed an executive order adopting key safeguards for the permitting of new sulfide-ore copper mining in the Boundary Waters watershed and directing state agencies to draft legislation that would make those protections permanent. In addition, Governor Walz’s order halts the permitting of new surface sulfide-ore copper mines on state public lands that would be located in the watershed. The order fills a gap left when Congress voted in April to eliminate a 20-year federal ban on the issuance of new mining leases on federal lands in the same watershed.

Following is a reaction from Andrew Wetzler, senior vice president for nature at NRDC (Natural Resources Defense Council):

“The Boundary Waters is one of America's most treasured wildernesses, home to clean waters and wild lands that belong to all of us. Washington sold out the Boundary Waters this spring to serve mining interests. Governor Walz's action today makes clear that Minnesota will not go along with it. When the federal government strips away protections for America's most iconic wild places, states have both the responsibility and the power to step in, and this executive order shows what that looks like.

“There is no fix for a poisoned watershed. Copper mining in the headwaters of the Boundary Waters poses an incalculable risk to clean drinking water, wildlife, and a recreation economy that supports thousands of Minnesota families. There’s no way to reverse the damage once it starts. The Minnesota legislature must now finish what Governor Walz started and lock in permanent protections so no future administration can trade this wilderness away.”

NRDC (Natural Resources Defense Council) is an international nonprofit environmental organization with more than 3 million members and online activists. Established in 1970, NRDC uses science, policy, law and people power to confront the climate crisis, protect public health and safeguard nature. NRDC has offices in New York City, Washington, D.C., Los Angeles, San Francisco, Chicago, Beijing and Delhi (an office of NRDC India Pvt. Ltd).

text:
This is a short post on what I believe an important subject for the Energy Industry. The title of this post is a bill being considered by the US Senate. The following is a summary of the bill by my Microsoft Bing Copilot browser:

American Energy and Mineral Infrastructure Act of 2026

The American Energy and Mineral Infrastructure Act of 2026 (S. 4944) is a Senate bill introduced on June 24, 2026, by Senators Alan Armstrong (R‑OK), Cynthia Lummis (R‑WY), Rick Scott (R‑FL), Katie Britt (R‑AL), and James Lankford (R‑OK) GovTrack.us+1. It aims to streamline federal permitting for energy and mineral infrastructure to address a growing gap between U.S. energy demand and outdated infrastructure.

Key Goals

Accelerate project construction by reducing delays from duplicative reviews, litigation, and political vetoes www.armstrong.senate.gov+1.

Ensure consistent, evidence‑based environmental decision‑making under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) www.armstrong.senate.gov.

Preserve environmental protections while making the permitting process faster and more predictable www.armstrong.senate.gov+1.

Major Provisions

FERC as Lead Agency

Strengthens the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s role as the sole lead agency for interstate natural gas pipelines and LNG facilities under the Natural Gas Act GovTrack.us+1.

Integrates water quality review into FERC’s unified NEPA process, incorporating state input and preventing one state from blocking federally authorized projects www.armstrong.senate.gov+1.

Clean Water Act 401 Review Reform

Streamlines the Clean Water Act’s 401 certification process for all types of infrastructure, reducing overlap and delays www.armstrong.senate.gov+1.

EPA Nationwide Permits (NWPs)

Expands EPA’s use of NWPs for linear infrastructure, eliminating duplicative review and extending permit terms www.armstrong.senate.gov+1.

Improves the “dredge and fill” permit process to avoid baseless lawsuits www.armstrong.senate.gov.

NEPA Clarification

Codifies the scope of NEPA review to prevent “boundless” environmental analysis and establishes meaningful judicial review www.armstrong.senate.gov.

Mining on Federal Lands

Provides statutory clarity to re‑enable essential mining activities on federal lands, benefiting hardrock mining and mineral producers www.armstrong.senate.gov+1.

Judicial and Procedural Reforms

Includes provisions to strengthen judicial review and reduce frivolous litigation that delays projects www.armstrong.senate.gov.

Rationale

The bill responds to rapidly rising U.S. energy demand from AI, advanced manufacturing, and industrial reshoring, and to global competition—notably from China’s infrastructure expansion www.armstrong.senate.gov+1. It targets over 4,000 miles of pipeline projects currently on hold due to permitting and litigation risks www.armstrong.senate.gov.

Support

The Essential Minerals Association and other industry groups have praised the bill as bipartisan, commonsense reform that would restore regulatory certainty for mineral producers and support domestic supply chains www.essentialminerals.org.

title: Big Tech's gas-hungry AI hubs risk blowing up climate pledges - Los Angeles Times
description:
The data center building boom has already strained the U.S. electricity system, prompting reliability concerns and moratoriums on new project approvals.
With even greenlit facilities facing years-long delays connecting to regulated electricity grids, data center developers are seeking alternatives.
The rush to capitalize on AI developers’ seemingly bottomless demand for computing power has produced some phantom projects and long-shot pitches.
The BNEF data includes projects backed by the leading AI labs, OpenAI and Anthropic PBC, upstart data center operators that fashion themselves as AI specialists, as well as cloud-computing giants and investor groups seeking tenants.
(Texas Governor Greg Abbott recently announced a pause in data center approvals.)
text:
Data center developers are turning to bespoke natural-gas power plants, a development that promises to dramatically increase carbon emissions and make it harder for U.S. technology companies to meet their lofty climate goals.

Ninety-nine proposed plants tracked by BloombergNEF would emit about 318 million metric tons of carbon dioxide annually if run at industry-standard rates, according to a Bloomberg News analysis. The entire U.S. electric power industry emitted about 1,485 million metric tons of carbon last year, according to Energy Information Administration data, meaning one slice of data center infrastructure has the potential to lift U.S. power sector emissions by 20%, and as much as a third should the new plants run flat out.

The data center building boom has already strained the U.S. electricity system, prompting reliability concerns and moratoriums on new project approvals. With even greenlit facilities facing years-long delays connecting to regulated electricity grids, data center developers are seeking alternatives. These include so-called behind-the-meter projects that can be permitted and built without the approval of utilities or the independent system operators charged with ensuring grid reliability.

“There is immense, immense pressure on the whole sector to get power, and get it fast,” said David Pomerantz, executive director of the Energy and Policy Institute, a utility watchdog that promotes renewables. “They’re sort of agnostic if it is clean or dirty.”

Not all of the proposed plants in the BNEF data are likely to be built. The rush to capitalize on AI developers’ seemingly bottomless demand for computing power has produced some phantom projects and long-shot pitches.

Bloomberg’s estimate of the likely emissions is based on 126 gigawatts of total planned on-site gas generation capacity tracked by BloombergNEF, an energy research firm owned by Bloomberg LP. The carbon footprint was calculated using a range of usage from an industry average of 60% to 100% for round-the-clock deployment, and a gas burn rate of a typical single-cycle gas generator. Emissions will vary depending on the use and the fuel-efficiency of the generator. A single-cycle model is now one of the most common types planned although it’s dirtier than combined-cycle plants that data center developers want but are struggling to get owing to a yearslong backlog for turbines.

The BNEF data includes projects backed by the leading AI labs, OpenAI and Anthropic PBC, upstart data center operators that fashion themselves as AI specialists, as well as cloud-computing giants and investor groups seeking tenants.

The projects tracked by BloombergNEF are spread across 22 states, from Alaska to Georgia. More than a third of them are in Texas, where ample oil and gas resources and a historically forgiving regulatory environment had developers rushing to erect data centers as fast as they can be built and powered. (Texas Governor Greg Abbott recently announced a pause in data center approvals.)

That includes plants backed by Amazon.com Inc. and Microsoft Corp., the largest sellers of rented computing power and data storage.

Earlier this month, Cleanview, which tracks U.S. power infrastructure and data center development, identified Amazon as the developer of an 8,000-acre site in Pecos County, which will become among the biggest single sources of carbon pollution in the U.S.

About 30 miles to the west, past a pecan orchard and scrublands dotted with oil derricks, Chevron Corp. is building Microsoft a gas plant to power a new data center complex on a 2,000-acre site.

The two plants alone could generate more than 10 gigawatts of electricity, enough to power New York City on a hot summer day. Their combined annual emissions may be as high as 45 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent, according to regulatory filings. That’s slightly less than half the cumulative emissions of Washington state, where both companies are headquartered.

That fossil-fuel infrastructure threatens to push Big Tech’s climate goals out of reach. Both Amazon and Microsoft are big backers of clean energy projects, and have said they aim to zero out their contribution to the carbon emissions responsible for a warming planet. Those pledges were made before the artificial intelligence boom, at a time when technology companies were under pressure from employees and outside activists to do more to cut their emissions. Spokespeople for Amazon and Microsoft say their climate goals haven’t changed. Amazon is exploring its options for solar power and battery storage at the West Texas site.

“It has been a remarkable shift in the last three years,” said Drew Wilkinson, a former Microsoft employee who organized his colleagues to advocate for tougher sustainability measures. “The companies who set the bar for corporate climate action are now bringing net new fossil infrastructure online at a breakneck pace. Few of us saw it coming.”

Dive Brief:

Hyundai Motor Group is bringing its existing V2X services together under a single global entity, called AllDayEnergy, that will serve as the launch point for future smart-charging and bidirectional-charging technologies in Hyundai, Genesis and Kia vehicles.

Drivers will see functionality through their respective apps. AllDayEnergy will be rolled out in Kia’s app for UK owners in the second quarter of 2026, with a planned expansion to Europe, the U.S. and Korea, according to a release from the automaker.

AllDayEnergy allows unified branding and software, with the automaker promising “a consistent and trusted experience across different markets and service types.”

Dive Insight:

Hyundai says that the AllDayEnergy name “reflects the Group’s vision of making smart energy management an integral part of customers’ daily lives and advancing its transition into a smart energy solutions provider.”

AllDayEnergy will initially cover smart charging, which will allow vehicles to charge at particular times of the day — and potentially at reduced power — that can altogether help reduce the load on public utilities, allowing them to emphasize lower-emissions sources, while drivers can take advantage of lower time-of-use rates.

Later, the service will roll out bidirectional charging to the home and to the grid, abbreviated V2H and V2G, respectively.

Hyundai has had its sights on bidirectional charging for many years. The E-GMP platform that underpins most of the EVs currently offered in the U.S. from Kia, Hyundai and Genesis was engineered for the tech, but taking advantage of it at home requires third-party hardware at present.

Kia currently offers a bidirectional DC wall charger from Wallbox that, with the installation of the accompanying grid disconnect switch, allows the EV9 or EV6 to become an energy storage device capable of providing home backup power or EV charging with solar energy.

Hyundai has already conducted several pilot projects in Europe utilizing bidirectional charging on the Ioniq 5 EV. And in November 2025 it announced the intent to expand smart charging and V2G in Europe plus V2H functionality in the U.S. — starting soon for the Hyundai brand with the Ioniq 9.

AllDayEnergy will face a unique set of challenges in the U.S. — most notably that there are about 3,000 electric distribution companies, or utilities, each with a different combination of rates, rules, regulations and permitting.

In 2024, BMW Group, Ford Motor Co., Honda Motor Co. and Nissan Motor Co. launched ChargeScape, a technology and services platform intended to start connecting utilities with EVs from those automakers’ brands and vehicles. Rivian, Tesla and Stellantis have since joined that effort, as well as several charging networks.

General Motors has its own separate GM Energy business unit to oversee energy management, stationary storage and bidirectional charging tech, including its own branded hardware. Hyundai hasn’t yet said if a unit such as this is part of the plan for AllDayEnergy, but the company does note that this signals a new identity for the company.

“When we launch AllDay Energy through our Kia App later this year, we will be taking a significant step towards establishing our identity as a smart energy service provider,” Woong Taue Hwang, VP and head of the EV Energy Strategy Group at Hyundai Motor Group, said. “We will continue to expand our AllDayEnergy service globally, allowing customers to seamlessly optimize their energy usage, reduce their energy costs, and contribute to grid sustainability.”

The biggest impediment, at least according to North America’s quasi-governmental grid watchdog, is power. “The only thing China is ahead of us in the AI race is power,” Jim Robb, the chief executive of the North American Electric Reliability Corporation, told reporter Arianna Skibell on the Politico Energy podcast episode that went live Monday. “We have better models, we have better engineers, we have better scientists — but we’re challenged in our society to build the infrastructure that’s going to be required to support the growth.”

2. Belgium battles its biggest wildfire on record

Europe’s hellish summer continues to shatter records. Just weeks after wildfires scorched Spain and France in what the French president called the country’s “hardest” challenge “since World War II,” Belgium is now battling its biggest blaze in recorded history. Hundreds fled as the flames approached the German border, though rainfall on Monday helped slow the spread. But the High Fens fire has already exposed political fissures in the country. On Monday, Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken blamed anti-American sentiment for preventing the government from purchasing Chinook helicopters that would have strengthened the country’s firefighting capacities, according to The Brussels Times, an English-language news website. In the Flemish-language Het Laatste Nieuws, the country’s most widely circulated newspaper, columnist Isolde Van den Eynde complained that the episode highlighted the gap between how much government infrastructure exists for climate policy and how little there is for actually dealing with warming-fueled disasters. “While quite a few citizens are wondering where our little army of climate ministers is,” she wrote, “soldiers are on the ground.”

Hawaii, meanwhile, was still reeling from the first hurricane to damage the Big Island in more than a century. Tropical Storm Lala, which strengthened into a Category 1 storm at its peak, knocked out power for nearly 200,000 homes and businesses across the state. As I told you yesterday, the utility that covers 95% of Hawaii has warned it could be months before power is restored. Today we got a clearer sense of the other damage. More than 100 homes were washed away in the storm, and the damage to roads and bridges, according to The New York Times, cut off access to a town with the only hospital in its region.

3. America’s oil giants eye Africa

Rwandan peacekeepers in Cabo Delgado.CAMILLE LAFFONT/AFP via Getty Images

Exxon Mobil’s oil fields off the coast of Guyana are booming, generating nearly $5 billion in profit last year and only expanding. Chevron last summer spent $53 billion to buy Hess and gain a foothold in the once-poor nation on South America’s Caribbean shores. It’s no wonder The Economist declared South America “the world’s hottest oil patch” last summer.

Now America’s oil goliaths are looking across the Atlantic for their next windfall. On Monday, the Financial Times reported that Exxon had revived its plans to build a liquified natural gas plant in Mozambique’s restive Cabo Delgado, despite the threat of terrorism from an Islamist insurgency in the region. At the same time, Chevron confirmed to Reuters the discovery of new oil and gas deposits in one of its blocks off the coast of Angola, the second-largest producer in sub-Saharan Africa.
