text:
At the peak of Japan’s bubble economy, a membership at Koganei Country Club outside Tokyo cost more than ¥400 million, roughly $2.8 million at the exchange rates of the day. Not the club. One membership. Golf memberships traded like securities in late-1980s Japan, and the Nikkei ran an index tracking their prices the same way it tracks stocks.

Then the bubble burst, and the country found out it had built golf the way it had built everything else in 1989: on the assumption that the line only goes up. The Nikkei Golf Membership Index peaked at 948.17 in 1990 and sat at 57.79 by 2002, about one-sixteenth of its high. Courses have been dying ever since. Japan had 2,154 of them left as of April 2025, a net 306 below the peak.

That collapse left a very specific kind of real estate scattered across the countryside: enormous, sunny, cleared, graded, drained, and already connected to a road. In 2015, a Kyoto electronics company looked at one of those corpses and saw a power plant that hadn’t been wired yet. And as of this spring, a wave of new Japanese restrictions on where solar can go has quietly turned that ten-year-old idea into some of the smartest land strategy in the country’s energy playbook.

Japan built more golf courses than golfers could use

Japan crossed 1,000 golf courses in the early 1970s and kept building for three more decades, peaking above 2,400. The sport was less a hobby than a business protocol, and during the bubble a club membership doubled as a speculative asset with a resale market and a price ticker.

The players went away faster than the courses did. Participation peaked around 12 million and had roughly halved by the late 2010s, before a pandemic-era wave of new and returning golfers pushed it back above 8 million, per the R&A’s 2023 participation count. The demographic math is still brutal: the bubble’s golfers came from Japan’s postwar baby boom, born 1947 to 1949, and that entire generation crossed 75 around 2025.

The asset side never recovered either. That Koganei membership was trading at about ¥60 million as of 2025, some 15% of its peak. A functioning 18-hole course sold for an average of roughly ¥810 million in 2022, per data compiled by Yanolja Research, which works out to around ¥45 million a hole. So hundreds of operators over the years have faced the same spreadsheet: keep mowing fairways forever for a shrinking, aging clientele, or find the land another job.

A fairway is a power plant that hasn’t been wired yet

In June 2015, Kyocera TCL Solar, a joint venture between Kyocera and what was then Century Tokyo Leasing, started driving racking into an abandoned course in Fushimi Ward, Kyoto City. The plan called for roughly 90,000 of Kyocera’s 270-watt modules, 23 megawatts of capacity, and an estimated 26,312 megawatt hours a year, enough for about 8,100 typical local households, per Kyocera’s announcement, with the power sold to Kansai Electric under Japan’s feed-in tariff.

Kyocera’s own case for the land was that dead courses offer “expansive land mass, high sun exposure, and a low concentration of shade trees.” Which undersells it. A golf course is engineered ground: the fairways were graded and compacted on purpose, the drainage was designed by professionals, the trees were removed from the playing lines decades ago, and there are service roads to every corner of the property.

Anyone who has followed what that prep work costs elsewhere can appreciate the head start. On a capped landfill in Houston, crews have to hold every panel down with concrete ballast because a single driven pile would breach the seal over the garbage. In Arkansas, the biggest solar project in American history is consuming more than 400,000 steel piles on raw farmland. On a dead fairway, you can drive piles all afternoon into ground somebody else already leveled.

The Kyoto plant came online in 2017 as the largest solar installation in the prefecture, and by the time its own financing partner described it in early 2018, it had grown into a 25-megawatt plant. There was a bonus layer of symmetry, too: Fushimi is the same ward where Kyocera set up its first major solar research center in the mid-1970s. Forty years of lab work, and the field test showed up next door wearing golf spikes.

Kagoshima never even got to play its course

The bigger project sat far to the southwest, on land straddling Kanoya City and Osaki Town in Kagoshima Prefecture. That site was zoned for a golf course more than 30 years earlier and then abandoned before anyone teed off, a bubble project that died as a drawing. Planning for its second life began in January 2014, after the local community itself pushed to repurpose the ground.

The announced version was 92 megawatts across 494 acres (2 million square meters), a footprint about the size of Monaco. The finished version, which began operation in May 2020, came in at 100 megawatts: 356,928 Kyocera modules, an expected 117,000 megawatt hours a year, and enough output for roughly 39,300 households by Kyocera’s estimate. Both golf-land plants finished bigger than announced, which is not a sentence anyone gets to write about construction very often.

It took real machinery to get there. Four companies, GF, Kyocera, Kyudenko and Tokyo Century, formed a dedicated operating company, the project cleared a year-long environmental impact assessment plus forestland development permission, and Tokyo Century arranged a syndicated loan with the Bank of Fukuoka and 17 regional banks. The result ranks among the largest solar plants on the island of Kyushu, sitting on ground that spent three decades as a paper golf course.

The model kept working after the internet moved on

The 2015 headlines faded, and the conversions kept going anyway. In April 2018, Kyocera TCL Solar completed a 29.2-megawatt plant in Yonago City, Tottori Prefecture, on 1.2 square kilometers of land originally designated for a golf course and other uses that never happened. 108,504 modules, an estimated 36,080 megawatt hours a year, power for about 12,000 households, all of it sold to Chugoku Electric.

Tottori was the harder test. It sits on the Japan Sea coast, with heavy snow and short winter daylight, terrain no one would call natural solar country. The company adapted the mounting design to the weather and built it anyway. A fourth site on the company’s repurposed-land list, a 27-megawatt project in Fukushima Prefecture, also sat on an abandoned course. With Yonago finished, this one joint venture counted 63 plants across Japan totaling roughly 215 megawatts since its founding in 2012, a chunk of it on land golf left behind.

Here’s the part with a twist of irony. Kyocera itself has since pulled back from making the hardware: it shut its Tianjin module factory in 2023 under pricing pressure from Chinese manufacturers, leaving a single domestic panel plant, and Nikkei reported the company had decided to retreat from the panel business. The fairway plants are on 20-year feed-in tariff contracts. They will likely outlast their builder’s panel division.

In 2026, Japan made this the only easy land left

To understand why this matters more now than it did in 2015, look at where the rest of Japan’s solar went. The feed-in tariff launched in 2012 rewarded output above all, and in a mountainous country with almost no spare flat land, cheap forested slopes got bulldozed for panels. According to economist Richard Katz, about 20% of Japan’s 9,200 utility-scale solar sites sit on formerly forested land prone to mudslides, and more than 230 accidents have occurred at such sites, one of which destroyed 120 homes.

Local governments revolted first. At least 175 cities, towns and villages passed their own ordinances restricting large-scale solar before Tokyo acted. Then the national government moved in one sustained push: a decision in October 2025 to rein in mega-solar by law, a Mega Solar Countermeasure Package adopted across ministries at the end of 2025, an amended Forest Act with tougher permits and penalties that took effect in April 2026, and a cabinet-approved bill on March 24, 2026 to tighten the Electricity Business Act on top of it.

Now hold that against the other half of Japanese policy. The 7th Strategic Energy Plan, approved in February 2025, wants solar delivering 23% to 29% of the country’s electricity by fiscal 2040, up from 9.8% in fiscal 2023. So Japan needs solar’s share of the grid to more than double, and possibly triple, while making it dramatically harder to build on forests and slopes. Every category of land that was already flattened, cleared and ruined for some other reason has become strategically precious. Golf courses are the largest single inventory of it in the country.

Nobody publishes a running national census of course-to-solar conversions, so the honest answer on the total is that documented projects span at least Kyoto, Tottori, Kagoshima, Fukushima, Hyogo and Okayama prefectures, and the closures that feed the pipeline haven’t slowed. The 306 courses already gone will have company.

The back nine pays the light bill now

The economics of the original plants are locked in for a while yet. Kyoto’s feed-in contract runs to 2037, Kagoshima’s to 2040, and the meters have been spinning through every policy fight described above, because nobody protests a solar plant on land that was scraped bare for leisure 35 years ago.

text:
For a long time, Tesla $TSLA seemed like the only real player in the electric vehicle market, and its models were everywhere. Over the past few years, other automakers have not only entered the market but thrived, and today dozens of electrics on sale deserve real consideration. Tesla ’s mass-market models remain common sights on American roads, especially near big cities or in areas with growing charging infrastructure, though they’re no longer the only EVs around, and sales of the high-profile Cybertruck have tanked, pushing it out of the top 10 despite SpaceX buying up a large chunk of production. Even so, Tesla still sits atop the overall sales charts.

The delivery numbers back that up. With plenty of manufacturers now building electric cars, SUVs, and trucks, something exists for nearly every buyer, and several models are selling in real volume. This ranking of the bestselling EVs in 2026 includes vehicles spanning a wide range of prices, from inexpensive smaller sedans to higher-end luxury vehicles with considerable power. The figures reflect the most recent sales data from the first half of 2026.

The 10 EVs below appear on U.S. News and cover the bestselling EVs so far in 2026. They span mainstream sedans, family-oriented SUVs and full-blown luxury vehicles, giving shoppers a genuine sense of how far the EV market has expanded beyond Tesla ’s early dominance. Federal EV tax credit changes have shaped much of this year’s sales picture, with several models on this list, including the Chevrolet Equinox EV, Ford $F Mustang Mach-E and Cadillac Lyriq, seeing meaningful sales declines tied at least partly to the loss of that incentive. Range and charging technology continue improving across the board, too, with multiple automakers adopting the NACS charging standard first popularized by Tesla and narrowing what was once a significant advantage for that brand alone. Together, these trends suggest a market growing more competitive by the month, even as Tesla continues holding its lead at the very top.

Credit: Tesla

The most popular EV on sale so far in 2026 is Tesla $TSLA's midsize Model Y crossover, with an estimated 163,454 units sold. It has outsold the number-two vehicle on this list by roughly 113,000 units in the first half of the year, buoyed by a 2025 refresh. The Model Y carries a U.S. News Rating of 8.5 out of 10 and starts at $39,990.

Despite that update, the underlying platform is old, though the Model Y still delivers incredible acceleration and deft handling, even if wheel and suspension options sometimes compromise ride quality despite 2025’s suspension updates. The EPA rates the longest-range Model Y at 357 miles, a distinctly respectable figure given the vehicle’s overall age.

The Model Y offers ample space for passengers in either row along with generous cargo room. A new Model Y L, which arrived this past August, adds a small third row and a larger cargo area. Interior build quality runs fairly mediocre, though, and Tesla ’s reliance on a giant touchscreen for many tasks can frustrate users who prefer physical controls. No Apple $AAPL CarPlay or Android Auto interface exists as a fallback for anyone unhappy with the native Tesla system.

Despite these shortcomings and an underwhelming new base model, the Model Y remains one of the bestselling vehicles in the U.S., including among gas-powered and hybrid vehicles. U.S. News’s Vehicle Testing Editor expects that trend to continue, since the 2026 version has only improved thanks to a midcycle refresh updating both styling and performance.

This mix of dominant sales and continued refinement gives the Model Y real standing as the clear leader among electric vehicles this year. Shoppers cross-shopping the Model Y against the new Model Y L should weigh the tradeoff between extra seating and cargo space carefully, since the third row adds bulk that may not suit every buyer’s daily driving needs.

Credit: Tesla

The Model 3 functions as Tesla $TSLA’s sedan and arguably its best overall vehicle, with an estimated 66,616 units sold. It rides lower than the Model Y, handles better,, and looks sportier, with a U.S. News Rating of 9.1 out of 10 and a starting price of $36,990. The Model 3 delivers quick acceleration and agile handling on twisty roads, though several German rivals still edge it out on outright performance. The EPA rates the Model 3 at about 363 miles of maximum range. Buyer interest has remained strong overall, though sales sit down 34.3% this year compared with 2025, according to Cox Automotive data.

The Tesla carries some notably desirable driver-assist technology. During testing, U.S. News’s Vehicle Testing Editor found the car’s Full Self Driving (Supervised) system navigated a wide variety of roads flawlessly with little input required, while noting the system isn’t fully autonomous despite its name, meaning full liability for the car’s actions still rests with the driver.

In keeping with Tesla ’s design ethos, the interior stays sparse, and the materials don’t particularly impress. Nominally a luxury car, the Model 3’s interior feels closer to a budget Volkswagen Jetta inside. Touch-based controls remain somewhat divisive, though a turn-signal stalk has replaced the steering-wheel-mounted buttons found on previous generations. Front-seat room and cargo space keep pace with the competition, though the rear seat suffers due to the sedan’s angled roofline.

This mix of strong performance and modest interior quality gives the Model 3 real standing as one of the most capable yet unpretentious EVs on the market. Shoppers drawn primarily to driving dynamics should test the Model 3 back-to-back against a comparable German sedan before deciding, since the gap in outright performance may matter more or less depending on individual priorities. This comparison matters most for buyers who value outright performance over brand loyalty alone. It also helps clarify whether the price gap between the two vehicles feels justified.

Credit: Hyundai

After the elimination of the $7,500 federal EV tax credit, Hyundai dropped the price of the 2026 Ioniq 5, which now starts at $35,000, with 20,730 units sold and a U.S. News Rating of 9.4 out of 10. The small SUV rides with genuine composure, offering excellent ride quality that stays soft in the best way. Drivers who want more performance can opt for the Ioniq 5 N, which delivers the most power and best handling in the lineup.

The Ioniq 5’s interior runs typical of many EVs, staying roomy with a flat floor and generous front seats. The interior design feels airy instead of cheap, since most touchpoints use quality materials throughout. Every trim gets dual 12.3-inch displays with wireless Apple $AAPL CarPlay and Android Auto.

Switching from a gas-powered vehicle to an EV requires some learning and adjustment, and the Ioniq 5 earns praise for making that transition considerably smoother by offering an easy, conventional experience alongside traditional Hyundai practicality, all without demanding drivers change existing habits or interfaces. U.S. News’s editor describes it as the electric SUV he most regularly suggests to prospective buyers.

This mix of familiar usability and genuine practicality gives the Ioniq 5 real standing as one of the most approachable EVs for drivers new to electric vehicles. Shoppers switching from a gas vehicle for the first time should prioritize the Ioniq 5 during test drives, since its deliberately conventional layout tends to ease the learning curve compared with more radically designed EVs. This step matters most for anyone unfamiliar with EV charging habits and day-to-day range management. It costs nothing but a test drive and can prevent buyer’s remorse down the road. This check matters most for shoppers who have never owned an electric vehicle before. It costs nothing but a bit of extra time and prevents frustration during the first few months of ownership.

Credit: Toyota

The Toyota $TM bZ received a simpler name and a refreshed look for 2026, and sales have climbed 89% this year as a result, reaching 17,553 units with a U.S. News Rating of 7.5 out of 10 and a starting price of $34,900. Intuitive tech, an enjoyable driving experience, and competitive range explain much of that jump, and a solid entry price paired with a decent feature set rounds out the appeal.

The bZ runs surprisingly spacious inside. Front- and second-row passengers get plenty of legroom, and while headroom stays generous up front, it tightens up somewhat in the back. Nice cloth and synthetic leather upholstery along with soft-touch plastic elevate the cabin, though dark, cheap-feeling plastic in other areas undercuts that impression somewhat. Overall build quality still runs quite well.

A boost in maximum range, now 314 miles, up from 252 miles in 2025, helps ease EV anxiety, as does the addition of a NACS, or Tesla $TSLA-style, charging port. Buyers should note that the base XLE trim doesn’t offer the longest range, since the bigger battery pack that delivers maximum range requires stepping up to the XLE Plus trim.

This mix of improved range and approachable pricing gives the bZ real standing as one of Toyota ’s most improved electric offerings this year. Shoppers focused on maximum range should confirm they’re looking at the XLE Plus trim specifically before finalizing a purchase, since the base XLE trim falls short of the vehicle’s full range potential. This distinction is easy to overlook during a quick showroom visit without careful attention to trim details. It also helps avoid the disappointment of expecting more range than the base trim actually delivers. This small check matters most for buyers who plan to rely on the vehicle for longer road trips. It also helps avoid a stressful moment far from a charger when the range is lower than expected. It costs nothing to double-check before signing any paperwork at the dealership.

Credit: Chevrolet

The Chevrolet Equinox EV shares its name with a gas-powered crossover, though it runs as a distinctly different, arguably better vehicle than its combustion-engine sibling, with 16,249 units sold and a U.S. News Rating of 9.0 out of 10. Every model offers at least 307 miles of range, where many electric competitors fail to crack 300, and pricing starts just under $35,000, making it a legitimate alternative to similarly sized gas and hybrid SUVs. The Equinox EV runs about one size larger than the gas version on the outside while offering similar interior room, and it stays comfy and well equipped throughout.

The EV also runs considerably faster. Two configurations exist: a front-drive, single-motor version with 220 horsepower and 243 pound-feet of torque, and an all-wheel-drive, dual-motor version with 300 horsepower and 355 pound-feet of torque. Neither configuration delivers especially engaging handling, though both feel notably quicker off the line than the gas-powered Equinox. The affordable entry price has helped keep sales relatively strong despite the loss of federal EV tax credits, even though sales are down 41% so far this year as a result. Chevrolet also recently brought back an in-house competitor, the 2027 Bolt, though it hasn’t been in production long enough this year to crack the top 10 EV sellers list.

This mix of size, value and improved performance gives the Equinox EV real standing as one of the most practical electric SUVs currently on sale. Shoppers deciding between the front-drive and all-wheel-drive versions should think honestly about typical driving conditions, since the extra motor and power mainly benefit buyers dealing with snow, towing, or frequent highway merging. This honest assessment helps you avoid paying extra for capability you may rarely use. It also saves money by avoiding an upgrade that wouldn’t meaningfully improve daily driving anyway. This tradeoff matters most in regions with harsh winters or frequent long highway commutes.

Credit: Ford

Ford $F eliminated some of the Mustang Mach-E’s standard features for this model year, though many niceties remain, with 11,632 units sold and a U.S. News Rating of 9.2 out of 10 at a starting price of $37,795. Sales are down 47% compared with the same period in 2025, suggesting some customers may have noticed the cuts.

Despite the reduced features, the Mustang Mach-E’s interior still feels quite nice, with comfortable seats and high-end materials throughout. The touch screen runs large with a crisp display, though physical climate controls would still improve the experience. Passengers in both rows stay comfortable, though space runs tight for three adults in the rear seats.

Some initially questioned whether the Mach-E SUV deserved to wear the Mustang name, but the sporty EV has proven it can uphold that legacy. Since its debut for the 2021 model year, the Mach-E’s hard-charging performance has proven itself worthy of the pony badge, according to U.S. News’s Senior Vehicle Testing Correspondent.

Buyers seem to agree. The Mustang Mach-E offers firm suspension, strong performance, and GT and Rally trims that add extra thrills for those who want them. Drivers more concerned with range can get up to 320 miles from the base model equipped with the extended-range battery.

This mix of sporty performance and continued brand credibility gives the Mustang Mach-E real standing as one of the most engaging electric SUVs available today. Shoppers who valued the previously standard features should compare current trim levels closely against last year’s lineup, since some amenities that once came included may now require an upgrade to a higher trim. This comparison often reveals exactly which features shifted and by how much across the lineup. It also helps buyers decide whether the current price still reflects fair value overall. This comparison matters most for returning owners upgrading from an earlier model year. It also helps set fair expectations before signing paperwork on a new purchase.

Credit: Rivian

The Rivian $RIVN R1S impresses through its utility and off-road performance, with 11,677 units sold, a U.S. News Rating of 8.6 out of 10, and a starting price of $76,990. It also rides with solid quality and good on-road manners. Anyone hesitant about the price should know it offers the best of both worlds, wrapped up with an exceptionally strong interior and a considerable feature set.

The R1S comes with three different power options. Two, three, or four motors and three battery pack sizes let buyers dial in what matters most to them: performance or range. The Quad-Motor version delivers a mind-boggling 1,025 horsepower rating, while the dual-motor setup with the Max battery pack achieves up to 410 miles of range.

Seating for seven people across three rows comes standard in the R1S. Though the third row runs tight, the first and second rows stay spacious throughout. The interior looks and feels distinctly luxury-grade, with roomy first- and second-row seating, according to U.S. News’s vehicle testing editor. The Rivian ’s touch-heavy controls can be polarizing, and it offers no Apple $AAPL CarPlay or Android Auto option.

This mix of rugged capability and genuine luxury touches gives the R1S real standing as one of the most versatile three-row electric SUVs on the market. Shoppers torn between motor configurations should think carefully about whether performance or range matters more day-to-day, since the Quad-Motor setup sacrifices some range for its considerable horsepower advantage. This tradeoff becomes clearer when you weigh actual daily driving habits against occasional long trips. It also helps avoid buyer’s remorse after choosing raw power over practical everyday range. This tradeoff matters most for families weighing weekend adventures against longer cross-country trips. It also helps buyers avoid overpaying for horsepower they rarely use in daily traffic. It costs nothing to think this through carefully before committing to a specific configuration.

Credit: Honda

The Honda $HMC Prologue, co-developed with General Motors $GM, stands as the first EV Honda sold in the U.S., debuting in 2024 as an initial hot seller before buyer interest cooled. Sales are down 48.5% from last year, with 8,407 units sold and a U.S. News Rating of 8.1 out of 10 at a starting price of $47,400. Honda has since made drastic changes to its EV and hybrid plans, and it will discontinue the Prologue after this year.

The Prologue offers sleek styling firmly in the traditional Honda mold, though it’s essentially a Chevy Blazer EV underneath, distinguished mainly by Apple $AAPL CarPlay. Handling stays refined and confident, and ride quality runs well throughout. Neither the single- nor dual-motor powertrains rank as the quickest in the segment, though both handle most driving scenarios with ease. The Prologue also delivers up to 308 miles of range.

The Prologue’s interior amounts to a bit of a mixed bag. Both rows offer ample legroom and headroom, and cargo capacity stays plenty adequate. The rear seats run a touch stiff, though, and hard plastics fill much of the cabin.

Still, a U.S. News reviewer praises the Prologue’s all-day comfort up front, noting that after several hundred miles behind the wheel, the front seat remained comfortable without causing fatigue or soreness.

This mix of solid comfort and an uncertain future gives the Prologue real standing as one of this year’s more bittersweet electric SUV stories. Shoppers still interested in the Prologue despite its discontinuation should factor resale value into their decision, since discontinued models sometimes depreciate faster than vehicles with a longer expected production run. This consideration matters most for buyers planning to sell or trade in within just a few years. It also helps set realistic expectations for what the vehicle might be worth later on. This consideration matters most for buyers planning to keep the vehicle for only a few years.

Credit: Lexus

The 2026 Lexus RZ has improved range and power over previous versions, and buyers have taken notice: sales are up a remarkable 106.8% this year, reaching 7,814 units sold and a U.S. News Rating of 8.6 out of 10 at a starting price of $46,000, according to Cox Automotive data. A strong feature set and good-looking styling help explain the jump, though the base RZ 350e still lacks some oomph with only 221 horsepower. Range stays merely so-so at 301 miles, and the interior doesn’t distinguish itself enough from its Toyota $TM siblings.

Even so, the interior uses premium materials throughout, and the RZ starts at a comparatively low price for its class. It runs roomy and quiet, fully earning its luxury designation. The switch to a NACS port for 2026 brings a welcome update for faster charging. Overall, the RZ delivers a great, quiet cruising experience with a comfortable ride.

Buyers hoping to upgrade to the RZ 550e F-Sport get more power and features across the board, though that upgrade comes at a higher cost, both financially and in terms of range, which tops out at only 229 miles on that particular trim.

This mix of dramatic sales growth and genuine luxury polish gives the RZ real standing as one of this year’s most improved electric SUVs. Shoppers deciding between the base RZ 350e and the upgraded 550e F-Sport should weigh the power gain against the range tradeoff honestly, since the more powerful trim sacrifices meaningful driving distance in exchange for extra thrills. This honest tradeoff helps buyers decide whether the extra power justifies the shorter driving range. It also prevents disappointment for buyers expecting the F-Sport to match the base model’s range. This tradeoff matters most for buyers who prioritize acceleration over maximum driving distance. It also helps buyers avoid disappointment if they expected the upgraded trim to match the base model’s efficiency. It costs nothing to compare both options before deciding.

Credit: Cadillac

Sales may be down 18.7% year over year, but the Cadillac Lyriq continues to impress new buyers, with 7,578 units sold and a U.S. News Rating of 8.6 out of 10 at a starting price of $59,200. It has also spawned an entire lineup of desirable EVs from the American luxury brand. As Cadillac’s first electric, the Lyriq stands as a distinctly world-class effort. Unlike many of Cadillac’s earlier comeback vehicles, it looks and feels special, with a beautifully detailed interior, and it drives exactly as a Cadillac should: quiet and relaxing when desired, but powerful and strong when pushed. That powerful side got a boost this year with the debut of the 615-horsepower, 650 pound-foot Lyriq V.

Plenty of desirable features round out the package too, from a large 33-inch dash display to a Super Cruise hands-free driving system, all at a price lower than electric alternatives from Rivian $RIVN, Mercedes-Benz, BMW and Genesis. Its considerable success has helped make Cadillac feel desirable again, boosting sales of the smaller Optiq and larger Vistiq models too. The loss of EV tax credits has hurt the Lyriq like many other vehicles on this list, though it remains a solidly strong pick overall.

This mix of luxury polish and brand momentum gives the Lyriq real standing as one of the most influential electric vehicles shaping Cadillac’s broader comeback. Shoppers comparing the Lyriq against pricier European rivals should factor in the Super Cruise hands-free driving system, since this feature often costs considerably more as an add-on elsewhere in the luxury segment. This comparison often reveals real value once you weigh the full feature set against the sticker price. It also helps buyers see past badge prestige alone when comparing similarly priced luxury EVs. This comparison often reveals real savings once you factor in every included feature. It also helps buyers feel confident they’re getting genuine value instead of paying purely for the badge.

text:
On a hot, muggy day, the long-awaited arrival of a 500,000-pound transformer in Dauphin County signaled “outward, visible progress” of Constellation Energy’s intent to restart nuclear energy generation at the former Three Mile Island plant for the first time in years.

“You can see a brand-new piece of equipment coming to the site … that’s going to connect the plant to the grid and to the transmission wires you see across the countryside,” said Bryan Hanson, the chief generation officer for Constellation. “This is the first, big component we’re having delivered to the site, and that’s the exciting part.”

The $9.88 million transformer from South Korea traveled from ocean liner to train to a specialized heavy hauler that inched its way along the final stretch through the island’s north gate in Londonderry Township just after 11 a.m. on Monday.

Three Mile Island was the site of a 1979 nuclear accident that transfixed the world. But after that partial meltdown in one of the plant’s two reactors, the remaining Unit 1 continued safely producing electricity for another 40 years.

In 2019, Constellation determined the facility was no longer economically viable and put plans in motion to permanently decommission the reactor. At the time, Hanson was the chief nuclear officer.

“We made a decision, a tough decision, to shut the plant down. And we had no intention of restarting the plant,” said Hanson. “For me, it’s exciting to see us restart the plant.”

The electricity generated will power Microsoft AI data centers, part of a $1.6 billion deal inked in 2024, and will support at least 650 permanent jobs.

The delivery is one of three transformers set to come to what is now the Crane Clean Energy Center, the last of which will be a backup. Each transformer will “step up” the 23,000 volts produced by the plant’s main generator tenfold, the level that’s “most efficient” for transmission lines.

“Our commitment still is the summer of 2028,” Hanson said about a restart date, though “we’re running ahead of that and we think in ‘27 we’ll be able to provide electricity.”

“This is the integral part between the plant and the grid to make sure the electricity can flow,” he continued. “Having that here already, this early in the process, makes us comfortable we’re going to be able to deliver our electricity on time.”

In a series of public hearings, several people have expressed their concerns about the restart, noting that the site would be only the second commercial nuclear plant in the United States to return to service after being closed.

But demand for power is surging, driven largely by data centers, according to electricity grid operator PJM. That makes the reliability of energy sources like nuclear important, Hanson added.

“All we’ve done is invest in renewables for many, many years, shutting down base load facilities like this one,” said Hanson. “This is one example where we’re undoing a wrong by restarting a plant that supplies 835 megawatts of carbon-free electricity around the clock, independent of weather, independent of pipelines.”

Senior Reporter Pete Hall contributed to this story.

description:
By Dan Murtaugh Chinese solar companies will go to great lengths to reach the US market: 20,000 miles in at least one case.
As detailed in this story, Chinese firms sent polysilicon wafers made on the mainland to Kenya and Nigeria, where they were wired into solar cells.

text:
By Dan Murtaugh

Chinese solar companies will go to great lengths to reach the US market: 20,000 miles in at least one case.

As detailed in this story, Chinese firms sent polysilicon wafers made on the mainland to Kenya and Nigeria, where they were wired into solar cells. Those were then shipped to Indonesia where they were pieced together into modules and marketed to the US as being of African origin, thus avoiding tariffs on Chinese and Indonesian solar imports.

The White House’s frustration with manufacturers’ ability to stay a step ahead of US trade laws finally boiled over earlier this month, when President Donald Trump announced a plan to target solar imports regardless of where they come from.

Equipment made outside the US will be subject to minimum prices all along the supply chain, from pure polysilicon to wafers to cells to finished modules. There will also be an additional tariff.

While that may be enough to put a stop to the catch-me-if-you-can game played by foreign suppliers, it remains to be seen whether it will be sufficient to help rebuild US solar manufacturing.

Trump’s new rules do include carrots for domestic producers along with sticks. Companies that commit to building new factories can keep importing equipment without the penalties.

But the president is also partially responsible for one of the biggest deterrents to investment in a US supply chain. American energy policy has whipsawed over the past decade, with the current administration favoring fossil fuels, making it difficult for manufacturers to gauge future demand.

Even if US firms do build solar plants, their products will almost certainly be more expensive and less advanced than those the rest of the world is receiving from Chinese companies.

In a world that desperately needs more power for growing fleets of electric vehicles and a surge in AI data centers, it’s a risky bet. US solar manufacturing needs to take such a giant leap for it to pay off that it will make 20,000 miles look like a short hop.

—Dan Murtaugh, Bloomberg News

text:
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit recently held that the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) likely improperly froze roughly $20 billion in clean energy grants and thus, repealed an injunction that kept the funds in place while the validity of the grants is contested in court.

By way of background, in 2024, the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund – a “green bank” created by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act – awarded roughly $20 billion to eight nonprofits with the aim of financing loans for clean energy projects. In early 2025, however, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act repealed the portion of the Inflation Reduction Act that established the bank, citing potential fraud and mismanagement. As a result, the previously awarded grants were terminated by the EPA, and the dispersed funds were frozen. Shortly thereafter, the nonprofit grantees sued, arguing, among other things, that the EPA violated the Constitution by failing to spend money authorized by Congress.

The resulting case, Climate United Fund v. Citibank, centers on whether the grant recipients challenging the terminated awards can proceed in federal court on constitutional grounds, or in the Court of Federal Claims under the Tucker Act on contractual grounds. While that jurisdictional question is still at issue in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, the parties have disputed an injunction established early in the litigation that froze the grantee-litigants’ access to the contested funds.

Regarding the validity of the injunction, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit held early last week, in a 6-4 decision, that the EPA likely acted unlawfully when it terminated the clean energy grants and thus, repealed the injunction keeping the contested funds frozen. The Court’s order instructed the EPA to allow the grantees to access the funds starting this week. However, soon after the court’s decision, the EPA and the grantees reached a deal to maintain the funding freeze while the issue is appealed to the Supreme Court, thus avoiding an appeal on the Supreme Court’s emergency docket.

name: Clean Energy
title: Prime Minister Carney announces the largest clean energy investment in North American history
description:
We have the natural resources, critical minerals, and clean power that will build this century.
Together, these projects represent the largest clean energy investment in North American history, at nearly $70 billion.
We are making Canada the best place in the world to build and invest in clean energy.
In a more dangerous and volatile world, we’re choosing to build clean, affordable, and reliable energy systems, in partnership with all Canadians, for all Canadians.
Related product Backgrounder: Prime Minister Carney announces the largest clean energy investment in North American history Associated links
text:
In a more dangerous and divided world, Canada’s new government is focused on what we can control: building a stronger, more independent, and more sustainable country.

Canada is starting from a position of strength. We have what the world wants. We have the natural resources, critical minerals, and clean power that will build this century. We have the workers and the ingenuity to turn that potential into strength. We understand we can build faster and bigger when we work together. And we have trust, the most valuable commodity in an increasingly volatile, unreliable world.

We have everything we need to build the future we want.

Today, the Prime Minister, Mark Carney, alongside the Premier of Québec, Christine Fréchette, the Premier of Newfoundland and Labrador, Tony Wakeham, and the CEOs of Hydro-Québec and Newfoundland and Labrador Hydro, announced a historic agreement to upgrade and expand the Churchill Falls Generating Station and develop the Gull Island project and related transmission, building one of the largest electricity projects in North America.

As part of this agreement, the federal government will provide $10 billion in federal financing to:

Upgrade and expand the Churchill Falls Generating Station.

Develop the massive Gull Island hydroelectricity project.

Unlock co-investment opportunities with the Innu of Labrador in a major new Labrador onshore wind project.

Build associated transmission lines.

Together, these projects represent the largest clean energy investment in North American history, at nearly $70 billion. They will generate 14,000 megawatts of clean, renewable power – nearly tripling the current generating capacity of Churchill Falls. That is enough power to light, heat, and cool all the homes in Toronto, Montréal, and Vancouver combined. These projects will support 23,000 jobs – from the skilled trades to engineering – and contribute $31 billion to Canada’s GDP through the early 2040s.

The Labrador Trough is a world-class mining region across Newfoundland and Labrador and Québec, with significant sources of high-purity iron ore. To harness this strategic asset and create high-paying careers for Canadian workers, the government announced the referral of the Labrador Trough Clean Power, Critical Minerals and Infrastructure Corridor to the Major Projects Office (MPO). The MPO will coordinate and structure federal financing, accelerate permitting requirements, and work with Indigenous Peoples to forge meaningful partnerships.

In addition, Canada’s new government will support strategic, pre-development projects in the Labrador region, funded under the First and Last Mile Fund (FLMF) through Natural Resources Canada. This includes the following projects:

Labrador West Transmission Expansion to assess the transmission infrastructure needed to connect critical minerals mining operations in western Labrador to the electricity grid, supporting regional opportunities and mine electrification.

Kami Iron Mine Partnership’s project to undertake planning and feasibility work for the transportation and energy infrastructure required for the large-scale Kami iron ore project near Wabush, Newfoundland and Labrador.

Focus Graphite’s project to undertake pre-construction work for a new transmission line and road connecting the Lac Knife graphite project to Hydro-Québec’s power grid, advancing the development of projects that will support the battery and energy storage technologies this country and our allies need.

SFP Pointe-Noire’s project to expand critical minerals handling capacity and related rail infrastructure, strengthening a key transportation gateway for mining production in the Labrador Trough.

We are making Canada the best place in the world to build and invest in clean energy. By combining the Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits, efficient project approvals, cooperation agreements with provinces and territories, strategic investments, and attractive financing, we are giving builders the certainty to build big and move fast.

Today’s agreement realises the enormous potential of Canada when we build together.

This is cooperative federalism at work.

In a more dangerous and volatile world, we’re choosing to build clean, affordable, and reliable energy systems, in partnership with all Canadians, for all Canadians.

Quotes

“Canada is extending its unique advantage in clean, reliable, and affordable power. Because when we master energy, we master our destiny. Through cooperative federalism, we are unlocking our immense potential, building big, building sustainably, building in partnership, and building Canada strong for all.”

“In the current geopolitical context, it is vital for every nation to secure its energy future. I am very proud to announce today the conclusion of this new agreement, which is a priority for Québec, particularly for generations to come. Through this partnership, we are supporting the energy transition and enabling the growth of our economy through renewable energy, while ensuring our energy independence.”

“This is a win-win-win for Newfoundland and Labrador, the federal government, and Québec. I want to thank Prime Minister Carney and Premier Fréchette for their leadership throughout this process. We are finally replacing the notorious 1969 Churchill Falls deal and the 2024 MOU with a new deal that will guarantee us more power, more value, and more transmission. Newfoundlanders and Labradorians will finally be the primary beneficiary of our own resources, with complete control over whether we use our power to develop our economy or sell to outside markets. Today is not about what we can tear up, it’s about what we can build up. It is now time for us to roll up our sleeves and get to work to build a better and brighter future for all of us.”

Quick facts

Today’s agreement is the largest clean energy investment in North American history, nearly tripling the current generating capacity of Churchill Falls. Together, these projects will deliver 14,000 megawatts of clean, renewable power, support 23,000 jobs in the construction phase alone, and contribute $31 billion to Canada’s GDP through the early 2040s.

The agreement advances:

Canada’s National Electricity Strategy, which aims to double the capacity of our grid by 2050 and supply clean, reliable, affordable power across the country for decades to come.

The Atlantic Energy Strategy, which was referred to the Major Projects Office in the fall of 2025. The Strategy focuses on developing renewable and non-emitting energy across Atlantic Canada – onshore and offshore wind, nuclear, and hydro – to meet rapidly growing demand across Eastern and Atlantic Canada and beyond.

Today’s investments strengthen the interprovincial grid and the export infrastructure that carry clean, affordable power and Canadian resources to markets at home and abroad.

The Labrador Trough is a world-class mining region stretching across Labrador and Québec. With significant sources of high-purity iron ore, it is a strategic asset for decarbonising global steel supply chains, reinforcing Canada’s leadership in both renewable energy and critical minerals, and giving Canada a significant competitive advantage in the transition to a cleaner economy.

Strategic, pre-development projects in the Labrador region will be supported through the First and Last Mile Fund (FLMF). The FLMF is backed by $1.5 billion in federal funding announced in Budget 2025. It supports infrastructure that unlocks new mines and moves Canada’s resources to customers at home and abroad. Recognising that most critical minerals deposits and enabling infrastructure projects in Canada are located on Indigenous territories, the FLMF makes specific funding available to enable Indigenous leadership, engagement, and participation throughout the mining value chain.

On clean energy, Canada already leads from a position of strength: the lowest residential electricity costs in the G7, the second-lowest industrial electricity costs in the G7 and the OECD, and the second-highest share of clean electricity generation in the G7. Today, approximately 80% of Canada’s electricity generation is non-emitting.

To build on that advantage, Canada’s new government is advancing strategic investments in the modernisation and expansion of the country’s electricity infrastructure, including:

Major Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits for clean electricity, clean technology, and carbon capture, utilisation, and storage.

Strategic financing through the Canada Infrastructure Bank (with a $20-billion clean energy target), the Canada Growth Fund, and the Indigenous Loan Guarantee Program (envelope doubled from $5 billion to $10 billion).

A new Productivity Super-Deduction, enhanced tax incentives covering all new capital investment, which allows businesses to write off a larger share of the cost of these investments right away.

title: Germany's Auto Giant Is Losing the Race | The Daily Economy
description:
Ford’s willingness to cut its losses stands in sharp relief against the decisions being made by Wolfsburg, Germany’s Volkswagen (VW).
Based on the EU regulators’ decrees for a 2035 ban on the manufacturing and sale of internal combustion engines, VW was forced to make politically generated malinvestments.
The question to be raised is a simple one: Were these management decisions driven by market signals provided by consumers?
The answer has been a resounding ‘no.’ Caught between genuine market signals and mandates from the EU, VW leadership chose to please regulators over customers.
While stateside job losses aren’t as stark as those at VW, they are nevertheless a warning sign to auto manufacturers of all nationalities.
text:
Automakers from Germany to Detroit are at a crossroads. Do they produce cars for consumers or for political points? Ford and Volkswagen are finding out what happens when they opt to please the latter at the expense of the former.

In its most recent earnings report, Ford registered a hefty $1.33 billion quarterly loss for Q2 of 2026 that was punctuated by a 10 percent decline in year-over-year sales for Q1 and Q2, along with a 4 percent fall in revenue in Q1. These lackluster results are partly the result of a failed electric vehicle battery venture along with the cancellation of EV programs that received an underwhelming consumer response. Surprisingly, Wall Street’s response was quite different.

Ford’s shares surged by seven percent despite the quarter’s losses. They rebounded in part due to Dearborn’s optimistic estimates for the rest of the fiscal year. Why the optimism? That rosy picture comes from the automaker’s realization that the road to profit is paved by the wishes of consumers, not politicians. The report acknowledged that consumers want big pickups and SUVs and haven’t been won over by Ford’s EV offerings.

Ford’s willingness to cut its losses stands in sharp relief against the decisions being made by Wolfsburg, Germany’s Volkswagen (VW). There, Europe’s largest automaker is discovering that the price for ignoring consumers in favor of Brussels’ mandates is lost market share, reduced productivity, and large-scale layoffs.

In late 2025, EU leadership announced sweeping directives for reaching all-time emissions lows. One of those requirements in the passenger vehicle market requires EU-based automakers “to comply with a 90 percent tailpipe emissions reduction target, while the remaining 10 percent emissions will need to be compensated through the use of low-carbon steel Made in the Union, or from e-fuels and biofuels.”

Compliance isn’t cheap. After the mandates were approved, VW CEO Oliver Blume announced: “Over the next five years, the Volkswagen Group intends to invest €160 billion. The focus is on Germany and Europe, in products, technologies, production facilities, and infrastructure.” Further, “ we are financing developments in future-oriented fields such as battery cells, software, and autonomous driving.” While not all of these new expenditures are purely driven by compliance costs, these regulations certainly steer capital toward politically favored investments instead of toward consumers’ desires.

This is a classic case of government-induced malinvestment into certain lines of production. Based on the EU regulators’ decrees for a 2035 ban on the manufacturing and sale of internal combustion engines, VW was forced to make politically generated malinvestments. The question to be raised is a simple one: Were these management decisions driven by market signals provided by consumers? The answer has been a resounding ‘no.’

Caught between genuine market signals and mandates from the EU, VW leadership chose to please regulators over customers. Unable to both comply with EU mandates and fend off further market share losses, the Wolfsburg-based manufacturer reversed course on the promise of new investments in July of 2026. They instead announced a 15 percent reduction in the original investment plan to about $148 billion. That’s not all that will be cut. In a recent internal memo, Blume warned that four plants and up to 50,000 additional layoffs may be in order on top of the same number of job cuts already agreed to by Porsche and Audi, amounting to a total loss of 100,000 roles. In response to the proposed cuts, labor representatives for VW workers — IG Metall and the works council — vowed to fight the cuts with their full might. Volkswagen’s labor force isn’t the only group feeling the pain, shareholders have seen the stock sink to its lowest level in sixteen years.

Wolfsburg’s decision to lean into costly EU regulations aren’t the only source of strain. Leadership also cited VW’s 20-percent cost disadvantage relative to its rivals, some of whom are newcomers to the European car market. New electric models from Chinese carmaker BYD have significantly lower labor costs. Meanwhile, US import tariffs have also put a dent in VW and Audi sales stateside, taking a 20 percent year over year slide in Q4 of 2025.

The first lesson to be taken from these outcomes is that it pays to keep consumers in the driver’s seat, rather than regulators, when it comes to management’s decisions on what types of vehicles to produce. The second is that more regulation means not only higher costs, but market confusion. Relieving automakers from such mixed signals is the surest way to speed toward profitability and satisfied customers.

Ford is now in a better position than VW in this respect, as the Trump administration has scaled back the Biden team’s more stringent Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) requirements. But there’s still plenty to be undone. The current administration’s estimates indicate that there would be $109 billion in savings to American carmakers by loosening emissions rules. Nevertheless, the rules still require that all US-made passenger vehicles make 34.1 mpg by 2031. That’s a significant reduction from the previous administration’s demands for mpg to reach over 50 mpg. Yet, consumers’ tastes for maximizing fuel efficiency have hit a wall.

This should come as a relief to Ford shareholders and workers, as the sales record for EVs in the US has been less than stellar. For every F-150 Lightning trimline sold, by way of example, Ford lost $44,000. In aggregate, that translated into a $19.5 billion loss on the project before the project was canceled in 2026. According to carbuzz.com, that massive write-down consisted of $8.5 billion for canceled EV projects, $6 billion for a dissolved battery venture, and another $5 billion for program-related expenses. Among EV truck competitors, the Tesla Cybertruck sold 7,000 fewer units than the Lightning and the Chevy Silverado EV sold roughly half of Ford’s 27,000 units.

As US automakers had been geared up to chase more aggressive CAFE standards, but also in anticipation of future, more stringent regulations, the industry as a whole made massive malinvestments in these technologies, which consumers haven’t adopted. As a result, throughout 2025, GM, Ford, and Stellantis slashed more than 20,000 US salaried jobs, or 19 percent of their combined workforces in the past year, leaving the Rust Belt even more oxidized than it was before.

While stateside job losses aren’t as stark as those at VW, they are nevertheless a warning sign to auto manufacturers of all nationalities. If pleasing regulators is job number one, then consumers, laborers, and shareholders get left in the dust. This stark reality reveals the high cost of intervention-based innovation versus consumer-driven innovation. The former artificially drives up costs with an unknown payoff. The latter still entails risk, but car manufacturers on both sides of the Atlantic have a far better track record of meeting consumer desires in the markets than in meeting those of regulators and bureaucrats, who are guided by the fickle nature of green politics.

text:
Plan balances reliability, diverse resources and costs while helping communities in the Carolinas continue to build robust economies

Near-term actions serve our customers' rising energy needs while keeping customer benefits, value and future optionality central to resource planning

GREENVILLE, S.C., Aug. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- South Carolina is one of the fastest-growing states in the nation, attracting new residents, major employers and billions of dollars in economic investment. Meeting the state's energy needs requires a reliable energy system that can support thriving communities while keeping costs as low as possible for customers.

Duke Energy's 2026 Carolinas Resource Plan – submitted Aug. 14 to the Public Service Commission of South Carolina (PSCSC) – reflects execution already underway and highlights new opportunities to power South Carolina's future.

The strategy is designed to maximize the value of existing assets while making prudent investments in additional diverse resources needed to serve the state's growing population and economy.

Through an execution-informed planning approach, Duke Energy will continue adjusting to changing conditions while maintaining its focus on delivering safe, reliable and affordable energy for Palmetto State customers.

Our view: "South Carolina's success depends on having the energy infrastructure in place to support new residents, new businesses and new or expanding industries," said Tim Pearson, Duke Energy's South Carolina president. "We've made significant progress executing the strategy outlined in previous resource plans, and this updated roadmap builds on that momentum and details the additional actions we need to take now to keep the Carolinas powered reliably and affordably as the region grows."

A plan for South Carolina: Consistent with previous resource plans and supportive of South Carolina energy policy goals under the 2025 Energy Security Act (Act 41), the latest plan advances new generation, new energy storage and renewables opportunities, evaluates future nuclear generation options, maximizes energy efficiency and maintains flexibility to adapt as customer needs, technology and market conditions evolve.

What's in the plan?

Key elements include:

Natural Gas: Natural gas is a major near-term reliability resource, with efficiency upgrades completed, multiple combined cycle (CC)/combustion turbine (CT) projects advancing, approval for a 1,400 megawatt (MW) new combined cycle facility in Anderson County secured, and turbine supply agreements executed with delivery beginning from GE Vernova in Greenville.

Storage: The company is scaling battery storage execution, with storage projects in service, equipment secured, interconnection activity underway, and an RFP for 400 MW of standalone storage in South Carolina.

Solar: Solar procurement and construction remain active, including completed facilities, projects under construction, and RFPs for solar and solar paired with storage.

Nuclear: Existing nuclear assets continue to be maximized through license renewals, uprates, and fuel-cycle work, while the company evaluates potential new nuclear options and considers sites in Cherokee County, S.C., and Stokes County, N.C.

Grid Edge: Grid Edge programs are treated as a core execution tool to reduce, shift, and shape demand through energy efficiency, demand-side management, load curtailment, customer programs, and storage demand response.

To explore more details of the 2026 Carolinas Resource Plan, visit duke-energy.com/CarolinasResourcePlan.

Our view: "As South Carolina continues to grow, we're continuing our investment not only in new energy resources, but also in programs and technologies that help customers use energy more efficiently and save money," Pearson said. "From energy-efficiency programs to demand-response initiatives and our grid modernization strategy, this plan provides customers with more value while ensuring we have the reliable energy infrastructure needed to support the state's future."

Maximizing value for customers: Duke Energy continues to use every tool available to manage costs for our customers while delivering the high quality of service they expect.

Through its proposed resource mix, the company is maximizing the value that tax credits provide customers and finalizing the recently approved combination of Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress – efforts that together will deliver more than $5 billion in cost-saving benefits to the customers and communities the company serves.

Duke Energy has also applied for loans from the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) that represent potentially billions of dollars in customer savings as the company strengthens the electric grid.

What's next: The PSCSC will hold a hearing on the resource plan in April 2027 and issue an order by June 2027.

Duke Energy Carolinas

Duke Energy Carolinas, a subsidiary of Duke Energy, owns 20,800 megawatts of energy capacity, supplying electricity to 2.9 million residential, commercial and industrial customers across a 24,000-square-mile service area in North Carolina and South Carolina.

Duke Energy Progress

Duke Energy Progress, a subsidiary of Duke Energy, owns 13,800 megawatts of energy capacity, supplying electricity to 1.8 million residential, commercial and industrial customers across a 28,000-square-mile service area in North Carolina and South Carolina.

Duke Energy

Duke Energy (NYSE: DUK), a Fortune 150 company headquartered in Charlotte, N.C., is one of America's largest energy holding companies. The company's electric utilities serve 8.7 million customers in North Carolina, South Carolina, Florida, Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky, and collectively own 55,700 megawatts of energy capacity. Its natural gas utilities serve 1.6 million customers in North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio and Kentucky.

Duke Energy is executing an energy modernization strategy, keeping customer value at the forefront as it invests in electric grid upgrades and efficient generation resources to strengthen the system and serve growing energy needs.

More information is available at duke-energy.com. Follow Duke Energy on X, LinkedIn, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook for stories about the people and innovations powering its communities.

title: Arizona city and industry leaders look for new data center standards as public opposition grows
description:
That has some Arizona leaders looking for new standards for what acceptable data center development could look like.
Marcus Hassen, chair of the ASHRAE data center committee says their standards for data centers specifically are about 10 years old and needed updating.
While Phoenix incorporates some of ASHRAE’s data center standards in its building codes, it uses recommendations from 2022.
Gallego recently signed onto a pact with about 40 other cities around the world encouraging more stringent data center standards.
An industry trade group, the Arizona Technology Council says data centers are a big driver of the state’s $35-billion tech industry.
text:
As the number of data centers across the U.S. continues to increase, so does public opposition to them.

That has some Arizona leaders looking for new standards for what acceptable data center development could look like.

That public sentiment against data centers was highlighted at a recent protest in Phoenix, where resident Nile Bunger showed up to tell the Arizona Corporation Commission, which regulates state’s utilities, that it should not approve a 14% hike in electricity rates being requested by APS.

“The public are going to have to be at the brunt of making sure these corporations, these shareholders are getting profits,” Bunger said.

The power company says it needs to increase prices because their costs have increased, and they’re investing to meet the unprecedented demand.

The company says it’s also asking to raise rates for larger users — predominantly data centers — by 45%

In late July, it saw record demand 400 megawatts higher than last year’s record. An analysis of early information shows data centers made up half of that growth.

William Carter was among the dozens lobbying the utility regulator.

“I definitely think the data centers and large users should bear their own costs for whatever they want to do,” Carter said.

A pew research report shows Arizona is one of the country’s top data center hubs with over 180 either operating or in development.

Now, cities here are re-evaluating the standards they have to meet.

For years, many city industrial development standards have been based on those established by a trade group called the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers, or ASHRAE.

Marcus Hassen, chair of the ASHRAE data center committee says their standards for data centers specifically are about 10 years old and needed updating.

“It wasn't obsolete. It was still a go-to standard, and it was applicable,” Hassen said.

But with data center development accelerating, ASHRAE published a new standard last year. And now it’s creating an addendum to address overall water and energy use.

“You could be consuming little water at the site, but the electricity you consume-that's being produced at a power plant somewhere, right? And the generation of electricity, depending on your geography, that can be very water intensive,” Hassen said.

While Phoenix incorporates some of ASHRAE’s data center standards in its building codes, it uses recommendations from 2022.

Mayor Kate Gallego says the recent boom in data center demand means the city needs to go further.

“We want data centers to care about our local communities and invest in a way that creates benefits locally,” Gallego said.

Gallego recently signed onto a pact with about 40 other cities around the world encouraging more stringent data center standards.

Those would make sure the buildings aren’t built too close to residents, don’t cause pollution, and that fossil fuels aren’t used to power them.

“We want sustainable, clean energy to power it, and we want data centers to consider and protect our water supplies,” Gallego said.

And, beyond resource concerns, Gallego says lack of transparency has also led to community outrage.

“It's now pretty widely acknowledged that the data center community needs to do better about being a good neighbor,” Gallego said.

And protesters like Nile Bunger want regulators to take action to protect the public as data center development continues.

“Individuals are going to have higher electricity bills,” Bunger said.

The Arizona Corporation Commission is expected to decide on how much the state’s biggest power company can raise rates by the end of the year.

Meanwhile, in June, state lawmakers voted to pause tax incentives for new data centers for the next three years. But the state saw 113 new applications for developments in the weeks before the pause went into effect.

An industry trade group, the Arizona Technology Council says data centers are a big driver of the state’s $35-billion tech industry. The council’s President Steve Zylstra said in a statement that he doesn’t want to see the state abandon data centers.

But he acknowledged the moratorium could be a way for Arizona to figure out how to accommodate the tech buildings more responsibly.

description:
The corridors were the Lake Erie–Canada Corridor, the Southwestern Grid Connector Corridor and the Tribal Energy Access Corridor.
The corridors had been selected in December 2024 under the National Interest Electric Transmission Corridor program.
The Tribal Energy Access Corridor covered portions of North Dakota, South Dakota and Nebraska, including areas involving five tribal reservations.
It said the National Interest Electric Transmission Corridor program itself was not being ended.
A draft National Transmission Needs Study released in July said the administration’s energy program required a transmission system capable of moving electricity reliably and securely across regions.
text:
WASHINGTON — The Energy Department canceled plans to designate three multistate electric transmission corridors selected during the Biden administration, ending a review process intended to speed construction of power lines across parts of the Midwest, Great Plains and Southwest.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright said last week that the department acted after reviewing public comments from landowners, local governments, tribes and other stakeholders.

The corridors were the Lake Erie–Canada Corridor, the Southwestern Grid Connector Corridor and the Tribal Energy Access Corridor.

“Transmission policy must serve the American people — not special interests or a climate-alarmist agenda that drives up costs, worsens reliability and disregards the concerns of local communities,” Wright said in a statement released last Wednesday.

The corridors had been selected in December 2024 under the National Interest Electric Transmission Corridor program.

Federal designation can help prioritize transmission projects and provide access to financing and permitting authorities in areas where congestion or transmission constraints are found to raise costs or threaten reliability.

The Lake Erie–Canada proposal included parts of Pennsylvania. The Southwestern Grid Connector crossed parts of Colorado, New Mexico and western Oklahoma. The Tribal Energy Access Corridor covered portions of North Dakota, South Dakota and Nebraska, including areas involving five tribal reservations.

The department said the review found that the existing designation process had created confusion about the scope of federal authority and had not effectively advanced transmission development. It said the National Interest Electric Transmission Corridor program itself was not being ended.

The department said future transmission planning would be aligned more closely with state and local priorities, the administration’s affordability and reliability policies, and the 2026 National Transmission Needs Study.

Colorado Gov. Jared Polis, a Democrat, criticized cancellation of the Southwestern corridor, saying the proposal could have improved reliability, reduced congestion and helped consumers obtain lower-cost electricity.

“Just five days after the Department of Energy found that stronger connections between regions and power grids would reduce congestion and improve reliability, the Trump administration canceled a power corridor that could help do exactly that,” Polis said.

Will Toor, executive director of the Colorado Energy Office, said transmission connections with neighboring states were important to reliability and access to lower-cost generation. He accused the administration of taking actions that could increase electricity costs.

Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., welcomed the decision, calling it a “smart course correction.”

She said the canceled proposals had raised concerns among landowners, farmers and ranchers and said federal policy should protect private property rights and local input.

The cancellations come as electricity demand is increasing and the administration has promoted expanded transmission and grid investment.

The Energy Department said it closed a $1.6 billion loan guarantee to AEP Transmission in October 2025 for rebuilding or reconductoring nearly 5,000 miles of lines in five states.

In February, the department announced $26.5 billion in loans to Georgia Power and Alabama Power for generation and grid projects, including more than 1,300 miles of transmission.

It later announced a $1.9 billion funding opportunity to increase grid capacity and reliability and a roughly $3.3 billion loan to AEP Texas for more than 2,800 miles of transmission work.

A draft National Transmission Needs Study released in July said the administration’s energy program required a transmission system capable of moving electricity reliably and securely across regions.

text:
Next month, Endurance Energy will send Adélie — a 100-kilowatt geothermal generator named for a penguin — to an undersea volcano off the Oregon coast, tapping hydrothermal fluids that can reach 750 degrees Fahrenheit.

It’s the Seattle startup’s fifth deployment onto the ocean floor, part of founder and CEO Andrew Redd‘s bet that the technology can one day electrify entire cities.

“Addressing the clean power problem is a way to make significant, scalable impact,” Redd said. “It’s a fundamental of human life — people need power.”

Endurance is part of a broader race to harness geothermal energy — heat from water or steam under the Earth’s crust, converted into electricity. But while companies such as Fervo and Sage Geosystems focus on terrestrial sites, Endurance is the first commercial venture pursuing undersea sources.

Redd left an engineering role at SpaceX to launch his company in January 2025. Endurance’s headquarters sit on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union, in a building that once housed seafood processing, just down from Ivar’s Salmon House.

“There was a big crab on the wall. There were pinup pictures from the fishermen that would sleep out back,” recalled Nate Rodland, Endurance’s chief operating officer.

This summer, the team expanded across the street into a 25,000-square-foot concrete facility — it’s cavernous, like a parking garage with ultrahigh ceilings — where giant white tents now house separate R&D and manufacturing operations.

The space is bustling with employees assembling components ahead of the Sept. 7 pilot demonstration.

“Everyone is incredibly multidisciplinary. The challenge is incredibly multidisciplinary. That’s what makes it so fun and exciting,” said Redd, watching his team at work. He pointed to the company’s thermal fluids analyst, for example, who at that moment was assembling electronics enclosures.

The team’s roughly three-dozen members include 12 SpaceX alumni, plus veterans of fusion startup Helion Energy and space venture Blue Origin.

Here’s how the Endurance system works:

Drill a borehole: The team will drill a narrow hole a safe distance from active vent fields that will go about 200 feet into the seafloor to tap hydrothermal fluid.

Harness the heat: Hydrothermal fluid flows into a generator, heating a closed-loop refrigerant through titanium tubes until it boils and spins a turbine.

Reset: Naturally cold seawater cools the refrigerant back into a liquid state to repeat the cycle. The warmed water is released to the seafloor.

Move energy: The deployment next month will send performance data back to shore via Ocean Observatories Initiative’s Regional Cabled Array, operated by the University of Washington. Permanent installations will move electricity through undersea cables.

Control the process: Underwater, remotely controlled electronics are housed in oil-filled, pressure-balanced chambers to handle deep-ocean conditions.

“We kind of joke that everything we do is just heating, cooling and pumping,” said Aditi Bhatt, chief of staff, as she pointed out earlier prototype devices housed in Endurance’s original building.

Each unit is named for a sea creature, moving up the food chain as the generators grow — krill, silverfish, and eventually an orca pod. Adélie’s generating capacity would be enough to power a small neighborhood of homes.

The company touts the environmental sustainability of its system, which has a small physical footprint, creates limited noise, releases no toxic chemicals and emits no carbon.

Endurance has done four prototype deployments, reaching a depth of about 2 miles and temperatures up to 726 degrees Fahrenheit. The company has previously visited the Pacific Northwest’s Juan de Fuca Ridge, the Mariana Trough, the East Pacific Rise off Mexico, and the Kingdom of Tonga in the South Pacific Ocean.

While the startup has made rapid progress, the strategy faces real challenges: high pressure and corrosive conditions, mineral scaling inside devices, and the risk of costly repairs to seafloor machinery. And though many population centers sit near shorelines, the systems will still need expensive subsea cables to carry power over potentially long distances.

But the potential to tap a limitless source of around-the-clock, carbon-free electricity is attractive, and the company has raised $63 million from investors.

The next device, at megawatt scale, will power Endurance’s first commercial pilot, with the Kingdom of Tonga. Work on that begins as soon as Adélie is deployed, with the goal of shipping next year.

The pace aligns with Redd’s experience at SpaceX.

“I remember many times working on the next rocket before the previous one had actually launched, just because of how much you learned from the process of building something,” he said, adding that the team is inspired by their mission.

“The sooner we can get clean, low-cost power on the grid, the more people we’re able to help,” Redd said. “So we’re really driving with intensity.”
